utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. While we await the arrival of the witness, can I invite you to introduce to me any new personnel who appear. I think there's at least one change of personnel since we were here before. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second, there's no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English channel now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of General Lazarevic has been joined by Mr. Djuro Cepic as co-counsel and from now on he will be sitting in the courtroom with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. You are aware, of course, that the solemn declaration you took, what is now just over three weeks ago, continues to apply to your evidence until it finishes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac to continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. I will continue from where we broke off on the 15th of July this year. That is to say, before the court recess we talked about some of the conclusions you drew on the basis of investigations that you said were appropriate in your assessment. Is that what you said, that your conclusions were appropriately made?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I'm interested in the following. Do you know how many verifiers were on the Kosovo Verification Mission and do you know when they came to the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the verification mission began in October 1998; at least that's when the agreement was signed. I'm not sure exactly when the first monitors hit the ground. Of course they supplemented a team already in Kosovo, the KDOM, Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission. And to the best of my recollection the KVM mission had, if I'm not mistaken, it was 2.000 monitors, but I truly do not recall the precise figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So before the Kosovo Verification Mission, KDOM was there, the Diplomatic Observer Mission, that also involved a certain number of people. Is that right? I mean a larger number of people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, "larger number of people"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, let that be my question. How many people were on the KDOM mission in Kosovo; do you know?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, do you know that among these 2.000 people on the verification mission there were a large number of, say, German observers?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give you the precise breakdown by nationality, but I do believe that Germans were a part of the delegation or the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me if I say, in view of the number of the verifiers, that the foreign ministries of some countries, especially NATO-member countries, had relevant information about what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot speak to what governments knew or did not know in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, that was not my question, what they knew I mean. I'm just asking if you will agree with me that through their verifiers they could have had relevant information about what was going on in Kosovo, even before October 1998 and especially as from October 1998 onwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, do you know the relationship between verifiers and the governments of the countries from which verifiers come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The precise nature of the relationship I do not know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness isn't in a position to answer that question, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Abrahams --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, now I would like Defence exhibit PD1 to be shown on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean 6D1?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- actually, 5, 5D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see what you've got on the screen. Where is this evidence leading, Mr. Bakrac? What is the point that you're trying to ask the witness about, until I see whether in fact this is a witness who can deal with this sort of evidence you're trying to lead?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to put intelligence reports to the witness, intelligence reports of the countries involved that are quite contrary to what he reported about. I mean on the basis of which reports were made of the Human Rights Watch, that is. So on the basis of three or four 15-day tours of the area, where he either carried out investigations on his own or with somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, what you see before you is an excerpt from official documents obtained from the International Lawyers Association Against Nuclear Armament. What I'm going to read out to you are three brief decisions. II, intelligence reports from the foreign ministry of January 12, 1999, addressed to the administrative court in Trier. "Even in Kosovo an explicit political persecution linked to Albanian ethnicity is not verifiable. The east of Kosovo is still not involved in armed conflict. Public life in cities like Pristina -- public life in cities like Pristina, Urosevac, Gnjilani, et cetera, has, in the entire conflict period, continued on a relevantly normal basis. The actions of the security forces were not directed against the Kosovo Albanians as an ethnically defined group, but against the military opponent and its actual or alleged supporters." So this is a decision of the administrative court in Trier Az: 514 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number; it was read out too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IV, opinion of the administrative court of Bavaria of the 29th of October, 1998. "Status reports of the Ministry of the Interior dated the 6th of May, 8th of June, and the 13th of July, 1998, presented to the appellant in terms of -- do not allow for the possibility of collective persecution against the Albanians, even regional collective persecution -- even that cannot be established with sufficient certainty" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not really objecting, but I think for clarity. I think counsel is moving from bits to bits on the document referring to various extracts on various dates, and the e-court picture is not moving to where he's referring. So if he could take things step by step, one extract and then the next extract so we could see what he's referring to. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the point is well made, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I concur with what my colleague said, and I do apologise. At the very outset I said that this was paragraph IV of the relevant document, that is to say, the opinion of the administrative court in Bavaria, October 1998. Az: 22 BA 94.34252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have the relevant passage now clearly on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, to save time may I continue from where I broke off or should I start reading from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on from where you broke off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Violent actions of the Yugoslav military and police since February 1998 were aimed at separatist activities and are no proof of a persecution of the whole Albanian ethnic group in Kosovo or in a part of it. What was involved in the Yugoslav violent actions and excesses since February 1998 was a selective forcible action against the military underground movement (especially the KLA) and people in immediate contact with it in its areas of operation ... A state programme of persecution aimed at the whole ethnic group of Albanians exists neither now nor earlier." VI, the opinion of the higher administrative court in Munster dated the 24th of February, 1999, VI. "There is no sufficient actual proof of a secret programme, or an unspoken consensus on the Serbian side, to liquidate the Albanian people, to drive it out or otherwise to persecute it in the extreme manner presently described ... If Serbian state power carries out its laws and in so doing necessarily puts pressure on an Albanian ethnic group which turns its back on the state and is for supporting a boycott, then the objective direction of these measures is not that of a programmatic persecution of this population group ... Even if the Serbian state were benevolently to accept or even to intend that a part of the citizenry which sees itself in a hopeless situation or opposes compulsory measures should emigrate, this still does not represent a programme of persecution aimed at the whole of Albanian majority in Kosovo. As a matter of fact, if the Yugoslav authorities act -- reacted to separatist tendencies by firmly adhering to the law and through anti-separatist measures and if somebody due to that" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could we please have the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... and if somebody crosses the border this still does not constitute intentional policy on the part of the Yugoslav state aimed at persecuting national minorities: On the contrary" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, I think time for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I agree, Your Honour, but if you allow me just one more minute. There is just one more brief decision and then I'm not going to quote anything anymore. "February and March 1998 do not evidence a persecution programme based on Albanian ethnicity. The measures taken by the armed Serbian forces were in the first instance directed toward combatting the KLA and its supposed adherence and supporters."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the text will have to be read out slower. There are other booths working as well, not only the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the interpreters are asking that you read these passages more slowly because there is an element of translation involved that doesn't depend on a transcript already provided in English. There are other languages to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. If there is any justification or excuse for this I just want to save time, I don't want to waste any time, and I am creating obviously a problem for the interpretation and I'm sorry. Is it necessary for me to repeat what I've read out so far or may I proceed? And the last decision, VII that follows after VI, the opinion of the upper administrative court at Munster, March 11, 1999. "Ethnic Albanians in Kosovo have neither been nor are now exposed to regional or country-wide group persecution in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." So that is a decision dated the 11th of March, 1999, ten days before the NATO bombing started. Mr. Abrahams, can you explain to us how come your reports are so different from the intelligence reports of the foreign ministry of a serious NATO country like Germany?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to correct what I consider a misstatement on your part. You said that I had travelled to Kosovo two or three times to collect the information in our reports, which is not correct. I personally travelled there five times between the period of February 1998 and March 1999. In addition, we did extensive research after March 1999 in Kosovo and outside. So I want to be clear about that. With regards to this document, it is exceedingly difficult for me to comment without reading the text in its entirety, without knowing the context in which it is placed, and without knowing that evidence that was presented in the court cases that you refer to here, so I am going to refrain from commenting specifically. But in general I would say that I disagree very strongly with the conclusions presented in this material. I believe, as I've said many times, that there was a systematic campaign against the ethnic Albanian population or a failure to distinguish between combatants and civilians. I believe there were also crimes against combatants, such as executions. The one specific detail that stands out -- and again, there was so much read that it is -- we would have to go through it point by point for me to reply, but I do agree with the assessment that there was no fighting in the major cities as of January 1999 because at that time the conflict was contained primarily in the rural areas and the fighting came to the urban centres later by March -- well, in -- by March 1999. But if you would like me to reply in more detail to any of these specific points, we will have to go slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also very difficult -- I certainly find it difficult to see that these are actually decisions that you're quoting. I mean, the very last one is a good example because in brackets after the part in quotations are the words "thesis 1." Now, do you have copies of these decisions of the various German courts that you can make available to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. For the time being I haven't got copies because this is a document that I obtained just recently, three or four days ago. But it was obtained through appropriate procedure and we have all the relevant numbers, and the Defence will try to obtain all these decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you also tell us what the document actually is?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an excerpt, it's an excerpt, that the International Association of Lawyers Against Nuclear Armament compiled on the basis of a certain number of court decisions; that is to say, of decisions of courts in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is compiled by a body which has an agenda which is anti-nuclear, and these are selective or selected extracts from court documents. Is that a correct summary of the nature of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are excerpts from court decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can see why in that context where these are simply selected passages that it will be important for us to see the whole document because if the whole document bears out the idea that you're presenting that a German court came to a conclusion that there was no persecution against the Albanian population, then that would be an important piece of evidence for the case. But as it stands, it's a sort of disjointed document that doesn't really take us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I was just interested in this witness's answer because he will leave and we won't have an opportunity to put questions to him. The Defence is going to present its own case, the Defence case, and there will be enough time, I sincerely hope, to obtain all these decisions. The purpose of this was for the Defence to try to establish what the position of Mr. Abrahams is, in view of these completely different positions taken by individual states that had verifiers on the ground and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you said that you are not aware of this source. I'm just going to repeat that these decisions invoke intelligence reports of the foreign ministry of Germany. Does that change anything in your position?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without seeing those reports or understanding the context of this court, I cannot comment, only to say that the text you have presented on the screen now I am in disagreement with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Since you've just told us that you do not agree with such positions at all, I'm interested in the following. Can you tell me something. In paragraph 4 of your first statement provided from the 8th to the 11th of March, 1999, on page 4 of the English version or page 5 of the B/C/S version, that is P228, Prosecution exhibit. You said that you carried out an analysis of the indictment for Kosovo against Slobodan Milosevic and others. When you said "and others," does that pertain to the accused persons present right now in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I didn't say that I disagreed with this entirely, this document. In fact, I pointed out to you one comment that I agreed with. I said in general. But if we want to go through the points one by one, I can respond to you. In regards to your current question, the indictment included some of the defendants but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it is correct that you carried out an analysis for that indictment?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the Slobodan Milosevic et al. indictment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That indictment. So will you agree with me now that practically you are one of the authors of the indictment against Slobodan Milosevic et al.?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me what it means that you carried out an analysis for the indictment?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of my assignments was to examine the background section of the indictment which presented the history of Kosovo, context of the conflict, and to obtain the concrete documentation to support the historical arguments presented in the indictment. That was one of my -- one of my assignments -- that was my main assignment with regard to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And were parts of your historical background incorporated in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I directed the Prosecution to where they can find or how they might obtain the historical records and documents to support the claims in the background section of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You refer, Mr. Bakrac, to the statement of the 8th to the 11th of March, and you said in the English version this is on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my mistake. I apologise once again. It's the statement of the 24th of January, 2002, and the page is number 4 in the English version. In e-court it's page 12. P228.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 2228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is on page 4, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 4. First paragraph, the first paragraph, page 12 in e-court, and it's just before the subsection entitled "Kosovo history."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] But that you just told the Prosecution where they could seek proof?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed some of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not all of that question was translated. Could you ask it again, please, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you directed the Prosecution to the proof relating to the historical background. Does that mean that you didn't write any kind of historical background but that you just pointed the Prosecutor's office to where they could find evidence?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I don't recall the specific details of every day's work, so it's certainly possible that we had discussions on the best way to phrase a development in the history or the important events. For example, the revocation of Kosovo's autonomy was a complex process over a number of years and we would have discussed what were the key moments worth highlighting in the indictment over others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, are you telling me that you just gave oral indications, that you did not provide a written analysis of the historical background and provided that to the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would have been provided in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Abrahams. I would now like to just quickly cover some other questions relating to the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army. I would like to know, Mr. Abrahams, whether you know, since you were out in the field, that members of the Kosovo Liberation Army frequently wore civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware that members of the KLA persecuted their fellow Albanian citizens who were loyal to the Yugoslav authorities, they burned their homes, and persecuted them in other ways. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict we documented a variety of abuses by the Kosovo Liberation Army against ethnic Serbs as well as against ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we assume that you did not manage to investigate a large number of such cases, for example?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think our reports are very complete. They contain the major incidents and events that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, are you aware that some humanitarian organisations in Kosovo helped the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about some humanitarian organisations providing assistance in money or weapons and so on to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have specific information, for example, who acted in such a way, how they acted in such a way. I certainly heard allegations that individuals in organisations of a humanitarian nature were sympathetic to the KLA and were assisting the KLA. And in my professional opinion I do believe that is a definite possibility, but I do not have concrete evidence to prove that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Were there any foreigners amongst the KLA members? When I say "foreigners," I mean persons who were not from the Kosovo area, who were not from the area of Albania either, but come from other parts of the world. Are you perhaps aware of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what you mean when you say "a few," there were a few?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the precise numbers and I have no idea if we're talking -- I can't give you any exact figure. But the number is definitely small. In -- there were many, many allegations about a large number of Islamic fighters participating with the KLA. I know for a fact that there were individuals in the KLA, factions within the KLA, who supported accepting these fighters, so-called Mujahedin, because they argued that we must take assistance from any place that we can, building off of the experience of Bosnia. However, there were also a large number of people and other factions in the KLA that rejected such participation from Islamic militant groups and individuals. And in the end, this position won. So in the internal debates of the KLA, they made a specific decision not to accept any outside fighters from Islamic countries. And to the best of my knowledge, that decision was respected. In addition to that, there were a couple, and I say "a couple," I can't be more precise because I heard anecdotal stories of some individuals from European countries also coming to Kosovo to fight, but again these were very occasional, let's say, mercenaries and of a very small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, would you kindly explain how you know that the KLA did not accept Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the last four to five years, I have been working on a book unrelated to Human Rights Watch, which is about the history of Albania. It is a history of the transition from communism, and it includes a chapter about the Albanians' role in the Kosovo war. And in the context of research for this book, I interviewed many, many officials and individuals in both Albania and Kosovo. And it is from these interviews and this research that I learned this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you talked about the KLA members in civilian clothing. Are you aware that in 1998 over 80 tonnes of weapons were confiscated from members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that precise amount, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But in your statement you did say that after the fall of the communist regime in Albania, an enormous quantity of weapons were transferred to Kosovo, ended up in Kosovo. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, are you familiar with the information that during the Rambouillet negotiations, the Albanian negotiators wanted to secure the agreement of the local commanders in order to sign the agreement. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, since you do know that a large number of civilians -- that a large number of civilians were members of the KLA, that a large quantity of weapons ended up in Kosovo from Albania, and since you are aware of the fact that the negotiators could not sign the agreement without the decision of the local commanders, I would like to know if you would agree with me that this is contrary to your assertion on page -- I will tell you the page of statement P2228. Actually, it's page 11 of the B/C/S and page 12 of the English text where you say -- and that's page number 19 in e-court, where you say that the KLA -- that already in February 1999, based on investigations in 1998 you had proof that the KLA were an organised fighting force in terms of international humanitarian law and that you were a witness to more and more indications of uniformity amongst the ranks of the KLA. Isn't that contrary to the fact that in February 1999 the Albanian negotiators could not sign an agreement until they had secured the agreement to do so from the local commanders, different local commanders?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's contradictory at all. The KLA by that time, February 1999, had become a more organised fighting force, but I would hesitate to call it a highly organised fighting force. And in particular, the KLA was a very decentralised, it had a decentralised structure whereby the regional commanders had a high degree of autonomy and there was a relative lack of central command and control, so that the negotiators in Rambouillet needed to get the permission or approval of the regional commanders before making such a major decision as whether or not to sign the Rambouillet accords. And I would like to add one point. You mention here that a large number of civilians were members of the KLA, and I would not accept that, that assertion. There were many, many civilians who sympathised with the KLA, but to become a -- or maybe participated and assisted the KLA, but for me there was a distinction and a difference between a civilian and a fighter. So when someone picks up the arms, they lose their civilian immunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excellent, Mr. Abrahams. Are you aware of how many Albanian homes were armed in Kosovo during the time that you were conducting your investigation?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. But of course in this region arms are commonly held. Many families have arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. So if they are wearing civilian clothing and many families have weapons, then they are not civilians. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you have just said that possession of weapons is the distinction between a civilian and a fighter, and now you have said that you do know that many homes in that area did possess weapons. So why would you not agree with me then that these are not civilians in that case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt if you really need to answer that question. You've already said that when somebody picks up the arms they lose their civilian immunity. That's quite different from possessing them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, before the break you said in your statement -- actually, in answer to a question by one of the colleagues, that the police and the military constitute a legitimate military target. Does that mean that a policeman in New York or a soldier in America would constitute a legal or a legitimate military target for a terrorist?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on the context of the -- of whether hostilities were ongoing, but such an attack on a policeman or a soldier in America would be a crime. If it were to take place today it would be a crime prosecuted -- which could be prosecuted under US law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can you help us with a transcript reference for that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have the transcript reference right now. I can provide that later, but I think that the witness also agreed that he said that, that the police and the military constitute a legitimate military target and then he now has explained that to us. But I would like to put the question if that means that a policeman in Kosovo is a legitimate military target, as opposed to his counter-part in America, policeman or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First we need to clarify what time-frame we are talking about. In a period of armed conflict, a policeman can be a legitimate military target, but it depends on the role of that policeman. So a person performing traffic duties in Pec, for example, would not be considered a legitimate military target, but a policeman who is engaged in hostilities would be considered a legitimate military target. So the police is a somewhat grey area in the eyes of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that this applies to armed conflict. Can you please tell us what an armed conflict means, the sporadic attacks by the KLA which at that time were -- was described as a terrorist organisation by Mr. Gelbard. As far as you are concerned, were they armed conflicts at that time or were those attacks by a terrorist organisation against legitimate organs of the state? Could you please explain what that means to you?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position and the position of Human Rights Watch is that a state of armed conflict came into being from late February/early March 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question is a bit more complicated than that, Mr. Abrahams. There may be a translation point here, but the word you used in the previous answer was not armed conflict but hostilities, and you said that where a policeman was involved in hostilities he could be considered a legitimate military target. And now we've moved on to armed conflict. Can you, at least for my benefit, clarify this. Do you see a situation -- do you recognise the possibility of a situation that no determination of a -- of the existence of an armed conflict has -- can be made, but hostilities are such that a police officer could be a legitimate military target? Do you envisage that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. No, I do not, no. Just to clarify, the question as it was posed to me, I assumed we were talking about already a period of armed conflict; namely, from February/March 1998 on. And in that period, then a policeman would be considered a legitimate target if he or she were actively engaged in hostilities. Obviously that does not apply prior to late February 1998, when a policeman is not a legitimate military target. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That certainly clarified it for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It is a little bit more clear to me but not completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you after February 1998, attacks from an ambush or an ambush on moving police vehicle, does that constitute armed conflict or hostilities in relation to official state organs?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: After late February/early March 1998, in our opinion, in my opinion, there was a state of armed conflict in Kosovo, and actions by the state and the KLA during that time must be viewed within the context of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, I asked you whether after February when you say, according to you and your organisation, there was an armed conflict. Is a moving vehicle or a police patrol that was attacked from an ambush, that was ambushed, does that -- do those police officers constitute a legitimate military target and are they taking part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would depend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that question wouldn't help us because the statement begs a question. The vehicle could be carrying he traffic policemen that the witness has already mentioned. It's all a question of circumstances, whether there is actually ongoing hostility which would warrant action, is it not? And your question is posed on the basis that if these police officers were involved in -- of taking part in the fighting are they a legitimate military target. Is that question going to assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. My question was whether the policemen who did not take part in fighting, there was no action under way, and who were ambushed, whether they were a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the car you refer to was carrying policemen that were not actively involved in hostilities, then they would be an illegitimate target, yes, not a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Do you know, since you carried out detailed investigations, how many attacks against the police or the army were carried out in 1998?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number. We tried to obtain that information through our letters sent to the authorities. We were also in contact with the media centre in Pristina and presented as much information we had from the government side, but I do not know the exact number of attacks that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What would you say, Mr. Abrahams, if I were to tell you that in 1998 there were 2.768 attacks against the military, the police, and civilians, 1.774 were attacks on the police, 243 against the military, and 751 were against the civilians. So if we were to calculate that, it would come to six to eight attacks every day.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, like any good researcher, I would want to see the specifics. Again, it depends very much on whether these incidents involved legitimate military targets or not. But the overriding point is that my job is to document violations of human rights and international humanitarian law. Of course we need to understand the conflict to know who is attacking and who is being attacked, but my concern beyond the context is not to document legitimate attacks that involve legitimate military targets. And furthermore, we have consistently reported on the violations by the Kosovo Liberation Army in numerous reports. But I do not believe that any of those actions, lawful and unlawful by the KLA, justify or explain the extreme and systematic violations by Serbian and Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, are you aware that there were frequent violations of the state border in terms of illegal crossings from Albania into Kosovo and weapons were also transferred across the border in the same way?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've written in our reports, the KLA received most of its arms from -- through the Albanian-Kosovo border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would then it not be logical that the Yugoslav army would carry out actions on the border in order to prevent such illegal crossings by people and transfer of weapons?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "actions"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of all the activities that would prevent the illegal crossings of the border and the illegal transfer of weapons. Sometimes also there were skirmishes with firing on the border with these people who were crossing the border illegally and transferring weapons.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to make a distinction. My job is to distinguish between legitimate, legal actions and unlawful actions. So of course the armed forces of Yugoslavia and of course the police forces of Serbia have a duty, an obligation, and a legal right to protect the borders. There's no question about that. My issue and my job is how they do it, and it must be done in a way that minimises the impact of civilians. And again and again we documented actions, as you put it, by these armed forces that involved the clearing of villages, the separation of men and women, executions of men in these villages, and a litany of violations that I have documented in these reports. So I take no issue with whether they can do it; I take issue with how they do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you say that you established actions by forces. In your statement 2228 on page 6 in the last paragraph and the first paragraph on page 7, you say that on the 26th of September in the vicinity of Mlecani village you saw a convoy of military vehicles. These vehicles were moving along a main road. Does that, in your view, constitute illegal activity by the army?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The movement along the road in itself does not constitute illegal activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why then is this detail included in your report? I fail to see what violation is involved in connection with this movement on the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- we do not label such movement as a violation, but we present the information to provide a context for the fighting that took place in and around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When referring to movements, are you aware - and there is television footage showing this - that units of the Yugoslav army, when moving toward the state border, used loudspeakers to call on the population and the KLA not to attack the army, and that in spite of these warnings the army was regularly attacked while moving toward the state border and the security belt along the border?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: 1998. May 1998, that is.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have not seen the television footage of this, but it's possible such calls were made through loudspeakers. But again, this was an armed conflict. I am not denying that the KLA attacked Serbian Yugoslav -- Serbian and Yugoslav forces. I'm not denying that in any way. I'm not even denying that some of those attacks may have been unlawful. It was -- it was an -- it was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, are you aware that members of the KLA frequently used civilians as human shields, especially in situations where there were illegal border crossings going on and in other actions as well?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. In all of my research I never once heard an allegation that the KLA used civilians as human shields. What the KLA did do on occasion was put the civilian population at risk by engaging in military operations from within civilian -- from within areas occupied by civilians, within civilian-populated areas, which is also criticised in our report. But I never documented specific cases of human shielding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, you spoke about the incidents in Gornje Obrinje, Orahovac, Drenica. Would you agree with me that all these are areas where there was clearly KLA activity, intense activity?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- we would have to be more concrete to discuss the specific villages and precise towns you're referring to. But in the general areas that you mentioned, there was KLA activity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Do you have any information to the effect that in relation to the incident in Gornje Obrinje, the commander of the Pristina Corps ordered an investigation and the result of this investigation was that in the incident in Gornje Obrinje the army did not participate?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that investigation, no, and we never claimed that the army was -- participated in the Gornje Obrinje killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Can we say the same about the incident in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same? What do you mean by "the same," that the military was not present?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That they were not present.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Orahovac incident are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The one on the 19th of July or from the 17th to the 21st of July, nineteen-ninety --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have information about the presence of the Yugoslav army in Orahovac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. I am slowly drawing towards the end of my questions. In your statement 2228 on page 12 of the English version, in the second paragraph, you establish there were 11 humanitarian centres in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt. 2228 is a document which has several parts, I think, and it has each of -- it has two very lengthy statements, one of 14 pages and one of 19. So it would be helpful if you would clarify each time which statement you're actually referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do apologise. This is the second statement of -- which is 18 pages long. And it's page 12, paragraph 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You stated that in August the Serbian government opened 11 humanitarian centres and that a very small number of Albanians applied for assistance. Your conclusion is that the reason for this was that they were afraid because of the violence they had experienced. Mr. Abrahams, do you allow for the possibility that they were afraid of the violence of KLA members should they apply for help to the Serbian state organs? We said previously that the KLA perpetrated reprisals against Albanians loyal to the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams. Are you aware in the same context that the Albanian villages near Djakovica in the border area, and I'm referring specifically to the village of Korenica, asked for help from the Yugoslav army and MUP, asking for protection from KLA terrorists?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic spoke directly to the villagers of the Albanian villages of Bratusa, Rovina, Molic and provided humanitarian aid to those villages. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, at the end I would like us to clarify a detail you mentioned in your statement. The statement I'm referring to is the first statement of P2228, page 15 in English. I do apologise. Let me just check. I think it's the second statement. Yes, it's the second statement, page 15 in English. That on the 25th of February the Army of Yugoslavia announced the beginning of winter exercises in Vucitrn where the KLA held positions on Cicavica Mountain along the Mitrovica-Pristina road. Are you aware, Mr. Abrahams, that these were not exercises of the Army of Yugoslavia or manoeuvres; it was tactical exercises of the 125th Motorised Brigade attended by Captain Ferdinand of the OSCE. Is that the event you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, I'm having a hard time finding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I haven't got it either on page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also, although I think the witness is quite capable, perhaps -- perhaps -- perhaps if counsel is referring to some more obscure parts of his statement he might let the witness have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that may or may not be necessary, but we first of all have to identify the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave it's the second statement from the 8th to the -- or rather, the 24th of January, 2002. It's page 14 in B/C/S, and in English I noted down 15, but I do apologise. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I have the B/C/S version here. I cannot find ... That's page 21 in e-court in the English language, page 13 of 19. So it's page 21 in e-court, fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. It's page 13 in the hard copy, 13 of 19, and it's the fourth paragraph. So could you ask the question again, please, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware -- or rather, does your statement refer to the tactical exercises at company level of the 125th Motorised Brigade carried out in the presence of Captain Ferdinand of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the particular brigade involved in these exercises or manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You carried out detailed investigations. You mention exercises, and yet you don't know what unit of the army was involved. Is that part of your detailed investigations?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't conduct detailed investigations into the precise units or brigades involved in this case and we try to when there is a particular crime and we want to identify which units were involved. But in this case we don't have the specifics on who was active in these exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This means that the exercises were a legitimate activity. Is that the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no violation of the law in conducting an exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Lukic -- oh, I'm sorry, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Abrahams. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I along with my colleague Mr. Branko Lukic and case manager Ozren Ogrizovic today represent the accused Sreten Lukic. I would like to clear up a few issues before I move into my main area of questioning. First of all, sir, during your examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor you went through several letters that Human Rights Watch prepared and sent to various persons in the Serbian and Yugoslav governmental hierarchy. If I can ask you a general question first of all. Can you verify for me in a Human Rights Watch did not send any of those letters or in fact any letter to my client, Mr. Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent letters to all of the individuals and institutions that have been submitted here, submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if that group of letters does not include my client, would it be safe to say then that Human Rights Watch did not individually contact him regarding any of their communications?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact if the group of letters we have gone through during your testimony do not include any police organs or structures from the territory of Kosovo-Metohija, would it be fair to say that Human Rights Watch did not contact or advise them either?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is one of those letters was sent to the Serbian Ministry of Interior. So in my opinion that would include the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question was with respect to police organs and structures on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, my understanding is that the Serbian ministry has responsibility for Kosovo which is and was a part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, presumably you knew that there existed police structures on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija and that there were at least two or three international missions in Kosovo-Metohija that were in daily contact with organs of the police in Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware that Kosovo had a police structure, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yet no efforts were made to contact these people who were perhaps closer to the ground and would be able to better respond to your inquiries?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we approached the police in Pristina, we were repeatedly instructed to go to the local office, the secretary of information in Pristina, or to higher authorities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can turn your attention to your publication entitled "Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo." For the court officials that's Prosecution Exhibit P437, if we can have that up on e-court, and that would be page 16 of this proffered document by the Prosecution. Page 16 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I could direct your attention to footnote 1 on this page which is slowly coming up on the screen. In this document at this section your organisation identifies some 12 officials in various organs of the Yugoslav and Serbian governmental structures, including the police, that your organisation believed to be responsible for running the Yugoslav and Serbian government's policy in Kosovo and Metohija and for its response to the so-called insurgency in Kosovo and Metohija. Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, as I look through this list -- and I invite you to do so as well if you're not sure about it. But isn't it a fact that not a single one of the six accused here today is mentioned on this list as being someone responsible for the government's policy in Kosovo and Metohija, according to your organisation?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this list, yes, although this list was later revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, the other week when you testified before this Trial Chamber you seemed to hedge and deny that the OSCE publication As Seen, As Told was relied upon or cited in your publication Under Orders. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall how I precisely responded to that, but I can tell you that we did at times refer to and cite the OSCE report in our material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If, Mr. Ivetic, you're going to accuse witnesses of hedging, then I would welcome a specific reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Abrahams, in the transcript pages 910 and 911 you were asked by Defence counsel whether in fact you relied mainly on the OSCE report called As Seen, As Told, and your answer was: "No, that is not correct."

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the key word there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, hold on. Deny is fine, Mr. Ivetic, but there's no basis there for suggesting the witness is hedging.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise and I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in fact, sir, I've had an opportunity to review your document and there are no fewer than 55 distinct references or citations to the named OSCE publication in Under Orders. Does that refresh your recollection and allow you to amend your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in no way. First of all, I -- as the statement you read back to me from three weeks ago makes clear, I said "mainly." I deny that we "mainly" relied. We mainly relied on our investigations in the field with about 600 interviews. The report Under Orders does cite the OSCE material as well as other secondary sources. I have not added it up, but I trust your calculation. But we did not, at no time, use information or allegations or documentations from the OSCE report as the sole basis for our conclusions. We cited their material when it corroborated or rejected information that we had obtained. So it was part of the body of secondary sources that we used in preparation for this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you can find a suitable time to interrupt we'll have our first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will have just one question that I hope will have a short answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Abrahams, do you know of any other of these secondary sources which is cited 55 or more times in your report?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to review the material to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we take a pause and perhaps the witness can review the material during the pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you care to do that, Mr. Abrahams, or are you in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do have the report with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you have the opportunity, it would be helpful. We will adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Abrahams, I don't know if you had an opportunity or ability to check your publication Under Orders during the break. Have you in fact been able to do so?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a cursory examination, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And can you first verify for me that your cursory examination revealed that the OSCE report As Seen, As Told was in fact repeatedly cited, and I don't know if you can verify my 55 citations that I was able to count through my cursory review?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to conduct a count and determine -- verify your number, but it is true that the report is cited throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is there any other of these secondary sources that is cited throughout Under Orders with as much frequency as the OSCE report As Seen, As Told?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a series of official Yugoslav and Serbian documents, specifically the magazine Policajac, which is an official publication of the MUP, of the Serbian police. There is the magazine Vojska, which is the official publication of the Yugoslav army. There is the MUP web site, which we referred to in a number of places, and also the Politika newspaper which was from the ruling Serbian political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, would it be fair to say that these other sources that you've cited are types of publications where you would -- perhaps cited multiple articles from various issues of those publications. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Whereas the OSCE report we're talking -- all the citations refer to the exact same report. So as far as a single article or publication is concerned, the OSCE report is by far the most widely cited document in our report?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a reflection of the report's magnitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And while we're on the topic of the OSCE-KVM report As Seen, As Told are you familiar with the methodology utilised by that organisation in selecting interviewees and performing interviews to obtain their source material?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, I believe, correct me if I'm wrong, I believe in your direct testimony from Mr. Stamp of the Prosecutor's office you testified that your findings in Under Orders were of limited statistical value and that the results could not be said to be extrapolated to the whole population of Kosovo-Metohija. Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two separate points in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second point is the extrapolation, and that is correct because we did not conduct random sampling so that we cannot reach Kosovo-wide determinations based on the data. The first point, however, is that -- is whether our statistical analysis had a limited value, and I believe it had a very powerful value in determining or better understanding the patterns of abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I had the question improperly phrased. My emphasis was on the greater population as a whole. Would it be fair to say then that based upon your explanation here your report is not even of any value with respect to extrapolation to the population as a whole?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify. By extrapolation I mean that we documented statistically 3.453 executions by government forces against ethnic Albanians, and from that figure I cannot extrapolate a larger number, I cannot take that amount and give you a total. However, I can analyse those 3.453 executions and come to some very powerful conclusions from my perspective on the manner in which and the environment in which these executions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to clarify the position for the transcript, the figure is 3.453.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that's already in the transcript in the corrected form.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, the gist of this is, though, that your source material are interviews conducted with approximately 600 individuals and what they told you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So all the conclusions, analysis that is being performed is based upon just these 600 interviews?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the word "just" to explain 600, but that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As far as the primary source material from actual interviewees, 600?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned that you had not performed random sampling, statistical sampling. I presume that since you had the advice of professional statisticians in doing your report that you were aware of the limitations of your report because of the fact that random sampling groups were not utilised?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and that is why we include a section in the report entitled "limitations of the data."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's where I was going, sir. Now, wouldn't it be fair to say that the 600 or so interviewees which were interviewed by your organisation represented a extremely limited fraction of the entire population as a whole? Specifically I think I calculate it to be approximately .03 of 1 per cent of the Kosovo Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to take time and do the calculation to agree with you on the figure, but the -- it is the -- that the results of our statistical findings rely on 600 interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if another organisation such as the OSCE followed a similar method of obtaining interviews, that is to say if they did not utilise random sampling groups, would their report or conclusions suffer from the same limitation that you have specified for your report, that is to say a limitation with respect to extrapolation to the greater population as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, because the question invites the witness to speculate about the methodology of some organisation that he has already said he doesn't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I'm just asking him if the limitation he has testified that he does know about, whether that is something that is specific just to his report or whether it's endemic to the type of method that was utilised, whether it's something that is from the method that was employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I repel the objection to the question. I think the question is perfectly properly formulated. The only question is whether the witness feels able to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can try. I have not reviewed the OSCE report in many years, in a few years, but my recollection is that it doesn't attempt to provide statistical analysis in the way that we do. So that extrapolation is a technical term to suggest that the data gleaned from a limited body can be applied to the province as a whole in this case, which is different from the -- which is different from reaching conclusions based on testimony. And I don't believe that the OSCE report is presenting hard statistical evidence based on their findings, unless I have forgotten a section of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you do say you haven't reviewed the report in some time, so it is possible that that is a part of that report?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is but -- yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just ask you then a more general question. Would it be fair to say that if one interviews a smaller group than the whole and extrapolates to the whole without using random group sampling, that that study would suffer the same limitation on its data that your report has?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were attempting to reach statistical conclusions, then suggesting that a limited and not randomly selected group was indicative of the whole population, then yes. But not if it was based on descriptive testimony that explains what took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And where you relied upon reports or findings of other organisations in formulating your own conclusions in Under Orders, if those other reports utilised methodology that has the same limitation, your reliance upon that information would also inherit those same deficiencies, would it be not?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not say that we relied upon reports or findings. We made every effort to conduct investigations on our own by interviewing witnesses and collecting first-hand information from the field. We utilised the work of other organisations to help us complete the picture when we believed that those organisations operated in a credible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know that you've actually answered the question, though. If there was a report that also did not use the random sampling group methodology, would the deficiencies of that report be inherited by you when you cite to it to corroborate your own findings?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would again depend on whether we are talking about statistical results.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- well, can you be specific? Maybe I can answer your question more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about drawing conclusions and making conclusions about the population as a whole based upon interviewing a small fraction of the population and not utilising random sampling group statistical analysis.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on what conclusions they were reaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, just to clarify. Coming back to our 3.453 executions, we did not attempt to apply that figure to Kosovo as a whole, for example, to say: Therefore, X number of people were killed. But we took that limited body, the 3.400, and analysed it as a self-contained unit because it can provide very important information about the gender of victims, the age of victims, the place in which the crimes took place. So to answer your question would depend on what the organisation you're referring to was intending to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would agree with me, would you not, that you also cite throughout your report to various newspaper articles relating to the events in Kosovo-Metohija during the relevant time period?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times we refer to media sources, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would agree with me, would you not, that -- let's call them media sources as you have qualified them, they're not always very reliable sources of information, are they?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which media sources are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our reports we made a concerted effort to rely on when we used - and I retract use of the word "rely" - because we used media sources to corroborate information. We used sources that we considered to be reputable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's one way of looking at it, but even reputable news sources, let's say for instance American newspapers, I believe such as the New York Times reported in 1999 that Ibrahim Rugova had been assassinated by the Serbs, as I recall. Do you recall that being discussed in the media at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But in fact Mr. Rugova survived the war, did he not?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So to that extent, even legitimate or trustworthy, as you call them, media sources still have their flaws because they are journalists. They're not necessarily investigators or experts in various areas?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me on that, that therefore the value of media sources is not as great as, say, primary sources for information?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always tried to get the primary source, which is more reliable than a media source.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you help me out here. Are you agreeing with me or disagreeing with me?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I agreeing with you that newspaper sources are not as reliable as primary sources, yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have a question. Have you been adding bibliographical notes to your report? Did you add from where you got particular information, I mean entirely? You have been covering all what -- wherever you gathered it from in the bibliography?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can move on to another topic that was brought up in your direct examination by Mr. Stamp. If we could talk about these letters that were sent to various Yugoslav and Serbian government officials. I believe, and correct me if I'm wrong, I don't recall if it was you or the Prosecutor who intimated that this -- that these documents were sent to put the Yugoslav authorities on notice of the nature of crimes being committed by their forces. Was that something that you had stated or that the Prosecutor had stated?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you would agree with me, would you not, that the documents that were tendered, these letters from 1998, they don't accomplish anything of the sort, do they? They don't talk about any type of crimes being committed but rather are merely requests for information regarding very general facts. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I cannot imagine whether they were received as a manner of notification or not. The primary purpose of those letters was to obtain information about alleged violations to include in our report so that we included government views in our -- in our coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look -- now, first of all, of the -- I believe there are about five or six letters. They are essentially almost identical letters, are they not?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are similar letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: About 90 per cent is identical with specific items depending on whether it was sent to the army or to someone with respect to the police. Is that --

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to review to agree with your statistical conclusion, I won't extrapolate, but I do accept your general --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The premise?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific questions depended on the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, let's look at one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's call up Exhibit P543 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is I believe the letter that was -- that your organisation claims was sent to the Yugoslav secretary of information, Mr. Matic, on or about July 20, 1998. Now, sir, if you could -- and perhaps while the document is scrolling if you could look through that and if you could tell me or point to any -- any notice of any specific alleged criminal wrong-doing, such as violations of international humanitarian law, that are specified in this letter?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me a moment to review it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I would categorise the letter this way. This is -- we are informing the government that we are conducting an investigation into alleged violations of IHL, international humanitarian law, and that we are requesting information from them to clarify a specific number of concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yet you don't identify any specific or alleged violations of IHL that they would be on notice on, do they?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this letter was sent in the phase of research, so we had not yet reached the conclusions that we eventually released -- reached in the report humanitarian law violations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.
