I believe you've acknowledged in one of Human Rights Watch's reports that about 250.000 displaced persons of non-Albanian ethnicity, including primarily Serbs, fled their homes in Kosovo-Metohija during the period in question when the NATO bombs began to fall. Or I, pardon me, strike that. From the period of 1998 through the end of the NATO bombing that 250.000 Serbs had been displaced from Kosovo-Metohija or non-Albanians and some of them were not ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you direct me to the reference in my material?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would believe -- unfortunately, I don't have a page reference, but I do have a page reference later on for some of the other stuff. It's in our report relating to the NATO air-strikes. Once we get to that maybe I'll find a page number. But do you have knowledge of the fact that Serbs and other non-Albanians from Kosovo-Metohija fled their homes and became internally displaced persons as a result of a fear for their personal safety resulting from the NATO attacks and bombardments? Do you have any knowledge without getting into specific numbers or statistics?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you're talking about non-ethnic Albanians who left their homes in the period -- during the period of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have numbers, but I do believe that people did leave their homes due to the air campaign and the ongoing war. But even more left their homes after, when there was definitely a discrimination against Serbs after June 12th, 1999, which we have covered in our reports also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's focus on the period of the NATO bombing for right now for clarity. I believe that your organisation has amassed information relating to the scope of the human tragedy that resulted from the NATO bombing in Yugoslavia in general but more specifically relating to the province of Kosovo-Metohija. Is that an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have produced reports based on field research that documented the civilian casualties from -- as a result of the NATO bombing as well as human rights conditions in Kosovo after June 12th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe you testified in your direct examination the other week that a significant portion of all the NATO attack sorties took place over the territory of Kosovo-Metohija. Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our report documents approximately 90 incidents of civilian casualties in all of Yugoslavia, about a third of which occurred in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I want to take issue with you on. That's how you testified when the Prosecution asked you to testify on this topic, but I'm a little confused because when I read your report specifically Under Orders at page 40 in e-court, P438, it's clear that you state that -- your organisation states that 56 to 60 per cent of civilian casualties from the NATO bombings were on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija, which is considerably more than one-third?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said a third of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, of the incidents. So would it be fair to say, then, that two-thirds of the civilian casualties resulting from the NATO bombings took place on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 56 to 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that many of these instances or incidents where civilian -- what NATO calls collateral damage but which is really the loss of civilian life occurred in these very same municipalities that we've been discussing these past several days' worth of testimony?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to examine the report in detail to tell you where precisely those incidents took place in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, by way of an illustrative example I believe in appendix B of your report, civilian deaths in the NATO air campaign, do you recall an incident in Djakovica on April the 14th, 1999, when it was reported that 37 named Albanians, naturally Kosovar Albanians, and an additional 36 other unidentified persons were the victims of and were killed by the NATO bombings, and again these would be all civilians. Do you recall that incident, for instance?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a vague recollection, but I don't remember the details. And I'm -- frankly I'm a little surprised if there's one incident with 60-plus casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that was one day, one day in Djakovica those were the deaths that were registered. Perhaps you can explain. P703 is the exhibit in question on e-court. It's appendix B. I'll get the page number in just one moment. That's page 74 in e-court. Yeah, I've confirmed it's page 76. The date of the incidents are April the 14th, and it's there, that portion that starts: "Area between Djakovica and Decani," and it lists members who are known and 36 unidentified persons. So perhaps you can correct me. Was I accurate in stating that this is a summary of the persons who died in that area as a result of NATO bombing in that one day?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps not incident but one day?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In fact, we know that there were probably multiple instances where NATO bombs, either directly or indirectly, caused civilian deaths?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these -- for instance, this one day where some 60-plus persons died, that would be qualified as a very significant and in fact devastating day in the NATO campaign, would it not, in terms of civilian deaths resulting therefrom?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, this is one of the areas where we -- where we've heard you testify that people left during this same time period, that is to say after NATO bombs began, left the territory, and either left -- some of them left Kosovo-Metohija entirely. Now, what I'm asking is: You would agree that NATO bombing cannot be excluded as a cause for these people to leave their homes if they had a fear for their personal safety, given the fact that bombs were falling and that there were instances of many civilians being killed by these bombs?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can exclude it and I'll tell you why. There may be individuals who left Kosovo because they feared a NATO bomb, but I, in all the interviews that I personally conducted and in all the interviews that my colleagues conducted, not a single person claimed that was the reason, and conversely they gave detailed and consistent testimony on why exactly they were leaving and how in particular they had been forcibly expelled from their homes, villages, and towns. Furthermore, they explained to us a process that we dubbed identity cleansing, which was on the border with Albania or Macedonia, Serbian officials or Yugoslav forces took from them their identity documents, their identification, their birth certificates, and what not, which we interpreted as a way to restrict or inhibit their return to the province. And again and again these individuals explained how their area was surrounded, how the men were separated from the women, how at sometimes the men were at that point executed, and how the rest of the families were pushed along the roads where they were encouraged towards the border, usually the army was on the roads, and forcibly expelled from the province. And we determined no correlation between the areas of NATO bombing and the areas that were being expelled, forcibly expelled, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, this is based upon your knowledge of the 600 people that you interviewed, what they told you?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is based on over how many months, I have to count to be exact --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: If other people interviewed by other agencies reported that they did leave because of NATO bombing, then that is something that would not be covered by your survey. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to review that material to determine whether I found it credible or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if Ms. Mitchell of the OSCE told us that there were instances of people that testified to her that they left because of NATO bombing, would that be a source you would find credible?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, you previously had testified, I believe, that you did not have any knowledge of the KLA undertaking acts of violence or attacks upon civilians of Albanian ethnicity in the year 1999?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between -- in the months March through June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the months March through June 1999. Okay. So we're clear on that. I take it then that you did not have access to or information about reports submitted by the Serbian police in the terrain regarding information they had or reports of villages that had been attacked by the KLA and whose inhabitants, including ethnic Albanians, had been displaced?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period March through June --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the period March through June 1999.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. I take it then that you did not have access to or information about reports submitted by the Serbian police in the terrain regarding information they had or reports of villages that had been attacked by the KLA and whose inhabitants, including ethnic Albanians, had been displaced by the KLA from those villages in the time period from March to June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have access to that -- those police records, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact, insofar as you testified that the only inquiries -- the written inquiries that were sent were in 1998 and that you did not send any subsequent written inquiries, you didn't even ask for that information from anyone, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So would it be fair to say then, sir, that again this is an area where your report, as comprehensive as it is, is lacking due to not having all of the relevant information regarding the region that is being discussed?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police reports on the activity of the KLA during the period of the NATO bombing would have expanded the scope of our research. I would have gladly included it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Just trying to see if there's some questions that I can short-circuit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You would agree, would you not, that in order to have a full and complete picture in any circumstance it is always preferred and in fact even essential to hear both sides in a conflict, is it not?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, due to not having the type of information that I've mentioned several times here and that we've seen some examples of, your report does not fully present both sides. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt. This is about the tenth time we've had that question in various different formats. The witness has already indicated that he would not even know of the existence of these reports, and so it leaves him in an area where he needs to speculate if they existed what would he do. And the question has come so many times that I have to rise, although I don't normally object in situations like this, but we have time considerations in respect to other witnesses who have problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If time's a problem, I believe that I'm close to winding up my questioning, and I'm just asking for a conclusion now that we've gone through several instances where the witness has confirmed he has not had knowledge of stuff, and we have seen an exhibit detailing some of the stuff he has not had knowledge of, and I believe it's relevant to the matters that he has just been testifying to, and I'm just trying to find out whether in fact he will acknowledge that his report is lacking at least in one respect due to not having this information, which obviously since he doesn't have knowledge of it I'm not going to go through documents with him. But I can bring him through some other means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter for argument in due course. I don't think an answer to that question would add to our knowledge, so move on to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the NATO bombings, I believe that you indicated in your direct examination that you -- your organisation viewed the acts by NATO that led to civilian casualties as being violations of international humanitarian law. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to move, if I may, to the oft-cited so-called Operation Horseshoe, which was utilised by NATO or was promoted by NATO as one of the main justifications of its commencement of air attacks against Yugoslavia. And if I remember correctly, this was a claimed offensive plan by the Yugoslav forces, purportedly to encircle Kosovo-Metohija and expel the civilian population. Is my recollection accurate as to what NATO portrayed or promulgated with respect to this Operation Horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to answering that, I have one small comment with reference to your previous question, if I may address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The previous question about IHLs of NATO?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, about our requesting information from Serbian and Yugoslav authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're past that, Mr. Abrahams Deal with the question which you've now been asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm just reviewing the question. Yes. There was much speculation and comment about the existence of Operation Horseshoe, which ostensibly was meant -- was the plan to expel the ethnic Albanian population. I never uncovered evidence to suggest that this specific "Operation Horseshoe" existed as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In fact, to the contrary, you uncovered suggestions or evidence that in fact this Operation Horseshoe was a hoax that was faked by the German government to deflect growing criticism at home over the direction of the NATO campaign. Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you refer me to the statements that you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Under Orders, P438, page 86 in e-court. While we're waiting for that, sir, do you generally remember something along those lines without getting into specifics?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have to see it because my memory is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem. We'll get there. Again, that's page 86. There it is right in the middle, and I'll start with the sentence, you see that, sir, where it says: "A retired brigadier general in the German army, however, later stated that the claims of a plan were faked from a vague intelligence report in order to deflect growing criticism in German of the bombing."

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that media report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And -- so does that refresh your recollection as to whether or not you discovered indications that in fact Operation Horseshoe was a non-existent propaganda tool being used by one of the NATO countries to prop up support for the air campaign?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included this statement in the report because I felt these allegations were credible enough to merit their inclusion; namely, that there were strong suggestions that the certain governments, in this case the German government, was using the so-called Operation Horseshoe to mobilise public support within Germany. However, while I am to this day not convinced that "Operation Horseshoe" existed per se, I am firmly of the opinion that there was a systematic and coordinated campaign to expel large numbers of the ethnic Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, are you aware -- I'm sure you are, since you indicated this was included because it was a credible source, that the individual who uncovered this in April of 2000, retired German brigadier general Heinz Loquai, actually published a book regarding this where he detailed precisely what the true intelligence was, namely that the Germans were using general Bulgarian intelligence, which stated to the contrary that any activities that the Serbian military forces were planning intended to drive out the KLA and not Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your research did not go that far.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was the book published?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: April of 2000.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to ask a question, Mr. Abrahams. What was the criteria usually which you kept in mind while accepting certain statements to be credible and some statements not to be credible? I mean, you would be having a general criteria about it, because otherwise it will be capricious taking some and not taking the other. Could you dilate a bit on that so that we -- at least for my purposes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I cannot give you a strict formula. There is no way to say that this newspaper is credible and this one not. But we did try and rely largely on media sources that are - how can I explain it? - this may seem vague, but generally accepted to be -- to have large readerships and are -- have reputations as valuable sources. But that said, most important for us was to provide the citation in a footnote so that the reader himself or herself can then best determine how they view this source, because credibility is of course in the eye of the beholder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did you try to have it corroborated with or check the material which corroborated the information that you got? Because repetition is one thing, of course, but then corroboration means if two, three sources are talking of the same, then of course there is a sense that you would -- that there is credibility about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to make sincere efforts at corroboration. And I should stress we never relied on media reports when making allegations about crimes; we would use media sources we considered credible to corroborate in addition to multiple witness statements. But in this case I raised this because I felt it -- it introduced a legitimate point again about the Operation "Horseshoe" per se about which I never had found evidence to support it existed per se this particular plan, which is not to say that I don't believe there was a plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now, just to get back a point that we had touched upon before we took our last break. You had mentioned several areas where you had knowledge of attacks or activities by the KLA that were aimed at the civilian population, be they Serb or otherwise. Let's focus for a moment on the activities of the KLA vis-a-vis ethnic Serb civilians that inhabited the areas that they controlled. You had mentioned I believe Djakovica as one of the areas where the KLA had undertaken attacks upon the civilian Serb population. Could you expound upon that, and please give us an overview of some of these attacks or activities that you have knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Djakovica area, most of the incidents I'm familiar with are from the period of 1998, in the spring/summer of 1998, at which time the KLA exerted pressure and used violence against civilian populations in the area under its control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these incidents, how -- how many or how frequent are we talking about, or was there just one incident or were there several such instances in the Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to answer how many incidents were in particular. If I'm not mistaken, and I would have to consult with our reports, I believe that 198 people, both Albanians and Serbs, went missing during 1998. And that figure is from the International Committee of the Red Cross, but please, I have to check that number to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's okay, but what I'm trying to get at is given that number, whether it's 198, 190, 150, would it be safe to say that we're talking about more than one incident and just leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Abrahams, I thank you for your time. I think I have exhausted all the questioning that I have for you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in response to questions from my learned friends for the Defence that after the letters which were exhibited in evidence here you did not send any other letters?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in your statement you said that you made several attempts to speak with the Yugoslav authorities for armed security, internal security, under the VJ in Belgrade, but you were not permitted to speak with them in spite of your best efforts?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And then finally in answer to my friend Mr. Ivetic you said -- well, I think it was Mr. Ivetic, but in answer to one of the Defence counsel you said in respect to the MUP you also made attempts to speak with MUP authorities in Pristina, that's the MUP for Kosovo, but you failed to do so. Could you elaborate upon that. What sort of efforts did you make to speak with the MUP authorities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At various times we approached police stations in Pristina and other areas, and we were continually told to refer our questioning to the proper authorities. I would add also that we did have a researcher in Belgrade throughout the period of the NATO bombing, a Yugoslav citizen, who was following the war from Belgrade. And in, if I'm not mistaken, May this individual, an employee of Human Rights Watch, was summoned to the police station in Belgrade -- to a police station in Belgrade, I believe Stari Grad, where he was interrogated for five hours by the secret police. His passport was confiscated and the Human Rights Watch laptop was confiscated. He was also visibly and verbally threatened, after which time we decided that our colleague should no longer actively engage in research, due to the threats against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were shown a footnote from the -- from the Human Rights Watch publication, Exhibit 437. It's human rights violations in Kosovo. Well, you were shown the footnote. I won't belabour it by reading the footnote again. And the point was made that none of those persons named in the footnote which detailed persons in command positions or armed forces and police in Yugoslavia include any of the accused here and you agreed with that, but you said that later on that report was revised. First, then, as a matter of the record, you would agree with me that that report is dated 1998, October 1998?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And further, without going through all the reports, this is also a matter of record so I just lead straight to it. The names of the persons involved in the command and control of the force of the FRY and Serbia that were involved in the human rights abuses in Kosovo during the NATO bombing are also -- are named in the report As Seen, As Told -- Under Orders, I beg your pardon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that would be the section dealing with the chain of command in which you would name every accused here?

utterances.speaker: FRED ABRAHAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is page 10 of the exhibit Under Orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Abrahams. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal yet again to give it, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic, you have submitted a notice of objection to portions of Exhibit P2228, and in fact it's one of the items that make up 2228 to which you take exception. I think your objection is to the admissibility of pages, I think, 4 to 18 of the 19-page statement. Is that correct? Sorry, Mr. Sepenuk. Now, this builds upon an earlier point taken by Mr. Lukic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By our Defence, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what you're concerned about is the portion of the statement which gives an account of the historical and political situation within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you object to coming -- that coming in as a matter of fact, as it were, or even opinion from this particular witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I stress, Your Honour, from this particular witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, let me just clarify first of all with Mr. Stamp what purpose, if any, he would seek to rely on this particular portion of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The portion of the statement, as I understand it, that's being referred to by the Defence is that portion dealing with the history of Kosovo. And when we say "history," we speak of a brief treatment of the period 1974 to 1995 and then a more detailed treatment from the period 1995 thereafter. Now, insofar as that is history, since it is in the past, firstly, that period, particularly the period 1995 thereafter, is well within the area that the witness could speak about as matters of fact since he was -- he studied eastern European affairs, including the Balkans, and he lived there, researched it, and studied it for the purposes of his work. Secondly, most of this history is relevant to the case in terms of the context in which the offences that were committed later on in 1999 were committed in the same sense that the indictment has a section "general allegations" in which it appears the history, so does the pre-trial brief, to make a setting or a background for the circumstance in which the offences charged were committed. And secondly, there are some aspects of the history, the later part, the 1998 section, which in the Prosecution's submission clearly forms a basis for which a Court can, having heard all the evidence, make determinations in respect to the notice to each of the accused in respect to crimes that were being committed prior to the ones specifically charged in the indictment, and I'm speaking particularly about 1998. So those are the two main purposes for the history, insofar as it could be called history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the objection, though, is a bit more basic than that as I understand it. The -- a witness can present an account of a historical -- of the historical background to demonstrate his understanding of history, and I doubt if any objection could be taken to that because the Defence might then want to demonstrate themselves that he had a false impression of history, that his evidence might be undermined because of an inaccurate understanding of history. So his understanding of the historical background seems to me to be relevant in that context. But the second way in which this evidence may be used is to actually prove what happened as a matter of historical fact. And it's so that that I understand the objection is directed, on the basis that he is not an expert qualified in history to give an account on which the Trial Chamber might -- might rely. Now, do you seek to use his evidence perhaps in -- undoubtedly in conjunction with other evidence as evidence of historical fact on which the Tribunal might make a finding that a particular event for -- well, a series of events, for example, the dilution of the autonomy of Kosovo in which the Trial Chamber might make a finding about that, or do you simply use it as an indication of what the witness's understanding of these events was?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, with your leave, confer briefly in respect to that specific question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for allowing me the time. Clearly, as indicated by the Court, his -- it is relevant to his understanding of the period, but the Prosecution would further submit that it is relevant for a little bit of a second element, the different element that was raised by Your Honour. And that is if corroborated by other witnesses in the course of the case, then his evidence in respect to the history or the background events can be accepted by the Trial Chamber as evidence of those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: With your permission, sir. It's -- I want to comment on this for more clarity. First of all, it's no compulsion not to accept a single person's testimony. This is universal. If the man is sounding credible, well, then, his credibility is accepted, whether it's corroborated or not. Secondly, I must say, as My Lord has said, a person is a recorder of history and that for his own purposes he understands it. A person is a professional historian, Toynbee for instance, and so on. Now, he's talking of cause and effects of things. There the matter differs, but anybody else who is writing a chronicle and writing things in that order is only stating this happened that day, that happened that day. And if he's truly doing it, he has a diary, he has something else to talk about, well, that is different, and you have to kindly appreciate it in that perspective as well, and that is my view. And thank you for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, okay, carry on, Mr. Stamp. But before you do I should make it clear that we want to hear any submissions that are to be made on this at this stage. And while I don't envisage making a decision without at least some debate among the Judges in private, we'll do this fairly quickly. So now is your opportunity to say anything else you wish to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I go to the purposes again, I think I barely touched upon and maybe I should, without repeating myself too much, indicate that this witness is not testifying about history or the history of events that occurred 100 years ago or 50 years ago. The history that he speaks of primarily relates to the affairs of the Balkans of the former Yugoslavia from the 1990s onward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me give you an example from this. On page 9 of the hard copy I have, 9 of 19, the first full paragraph: "Human rights abuses in the province intensified towards the end of 1996 as the government attempted to quash the growing insurgency. Police acted with near total impunity as they maltreated and occasionally killed ethnic Albanians. Police abuse took -- generally took three forms, random beatings on the streets and other public places, targeted attacks against politically active ethnic Albanians, or arbitrary retaliation for KLA attacks on Serbian policemen. This period is documented in the report I researched and wrote. Persecution persists. Published in December 1996." Now, do you think that the Trial Chamber should be invited on that basis to make findings in fact about the way in which the police acted in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This witness is ideally suited to speak about the human rights situation in Yugoslavia, in Kosovo in particular, since, as he testified from 1993, that area and that specific type of inquiry was the focus of his academic work, his studies, and his research. So he is not speaking of history in the academic sense; he is speaking of the affairs of that country and that part of that country that he himself was involved in investigating personally as somebody who had done a master's degree in that field, not only specifically the area, eastern Europe and the Balkans, but also human rights studies. And not only had he done that academically, but he was there on the ground doing the research. So insofar as that is an issue which -- and it is probably an issue which to a limited degree might concern the Court. Insofar as there is that issue, this is one source that the Court, it is my submission, could use to come to a decision on that issue. Indeed, I'm reminded that that very year, according to his statement, he was there in Kosovo in the field doing research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Sorry. Is there anything else you would like to add on any aspect of this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Sepenuk, do you wish to supplement what you've submitted in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just very briefly. I'd like to add -- Your Honour read from page 9, the first paragraph of this 19-page report, the statement of 24 January 2002. There are other indications in that report, Your Honour, that -- that Mr. Abrahams is giving opinions and conclusions that simply should be inadmissible in this case. Can I just give a few more? For example, on page 8 of this 19-page statement he says in the middle of the page: "By mid-1996 I documented a clear pattern of arbitrary and indiscriminate retaliation by the Serbian police and special security forces against ethnic Albanians who lived in the areas where KLA attacks were taking place. Police broke into private homes without warrants and detained ethnic Albanians, often abusing them physically, et cetera." Another example, Your Honour. By the way, he speaks also about the Racak incident on page 13 of this 19-page statement, which has been excluded by Your Honours in the case. But he says on page 14 under the period -- the period of NATO bombing right in the middle of the page: "With the withdrawal of the KVM monitors, Serbian and Yugoslav forces implemented a coordinated campaign to expel large numbers of ethnic Albanians from Kosovo." And he goes on to say on page 15 of this 19-page statement, the last full paragraph: "The forced expulsion was well-organised. Refugees were driven into flight or were transported in state-organised transportation to the borders in a concerted programme of forced expulsion and deportation characterised by a very high degree of coordination and control." Well, Your Honour, that could be Mr. Hannis or Mr. Stamp making their closing arguments in this case, or indeed making their opening statements in this case. And the irony of this, Your Honour, is that Mr. Stamp in his submission, Mr. Hannis and Mr. Stamp in their submission on the report As Seen, As Told state as one of the justifications for admitting the report that these reports contain "recitations of witness accounts or otherwise relayed or observed facts rather than conclusions or opinions." Well, the fact is that those two reports contain all sorts of opinions and conclusions, and needless to say this is what purports to be objective dispassionate history contains these conclusions and opinions of the witness that are really totally inadmissible. One was read by Your Honour, now we have read several, based upon 600 interviews which to this day we have not seen. We have not seen a single one of those unsworn cross-examined interviews. So I think that his -- and his bias for the Prosecution. And forgive me, because the man has obviously done fine work. He's well-intentioned, he's a human rights activist. I'm glad he's on the planet, but he shouldn't be here, and he is here as an advocate for the Prosecution, not as a dispassionate witness. He's worked for the Prosecution, he's done analysis for them. And as you'll recall from my cross-examination about Mr. Milosevic, he said as early as I think it was February, or August, I forget, in 1998, he says the first priority, not one of the priorities, the first priority of American foreign policy should be the indictment of President Milosevic. So this man is an advocate; he's not a dispassionate witness. He really just for nothing else than the appearance of impropriety, he purports to give, you know, this history, this cool, dispassionate survey of history. You know, he gave that to the Prosecution for their background part of the indictment, and now he's giving it here to you. And human activists, good as they are, well-intentioned as they are, should really have no role in determining the ultimate outcome of this case which will be determined by Your Honours. Therefore, we say that this entire statement should not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Ivetic, do you have anything to add to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll just very briefly add to what my colleague has said, and I'll limit my comments to this particular exhibit rather than the objections we have to Under Orders as well. The main problem is as we saw through his testimony is that a lot of his conclusions and findings are based upon the information he had at hand and that is not necessarily the totality of the information available. Given that this information in his Rule 89(F) statement is culled from his various reports, we do not know what portions are the result of things that he actually eye-witnessed or did research on and what was written by somebody else, or what he heard from somebody, what he heard from an interviewee, for instance. So it's very difficult to discern what is first-hand history that he experienced and which he could report upon, and what is second-hand history that he is reciting from some other source of which since we don't even know who that source is we have no idea about the credibility or the credentials of the same. And so in that instance I do not think that this type of documentary testimony can be taken for the second purpose, that is to say, to have the Court -- have that proved to the Court the factual backdrop that is relevant to these proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that you accept that the evidence is all relevant to establish his understanding of what the history --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: His belief and his understanding, I think, you know, that is correct. And again the limitations of his belief and his understanding as well, if we show that to be. And then I just had one issue of a -- more of a question really. I believe Mr. Stamp indicated that this was the focus of his academic work and that the research he was doing on the ground was part of an academic work. I don't recall any testimony of that, so if that's what's being presented here, I would object to that. I think it was very clear that this was -- this was his -- he was not part of any academic endeavour, so that there would not have been any academic review, et cetera, of these items. And without that, I think the applicability of this evidence to the second prong is really non-existent, or not appropriate I should say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, your original objection was to the admissibility of this -- of the report Under Orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that you said was for the same reason as your objection to As Seen, As Told.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And now that we have submitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, now that we've submitted the written brief on As Seen, As Told I think the same parallels and arguments apply. That namely, it is my understanding and my belief from the testimony that was elicited from this witness that it's very clear that one of the main objectives of his work in interviewing these people was to obtain information for the assistance of the prosecution of war crimes before this Tribunal. And therefore I believe it very squarely falls within the grounds of the Milosevic appeals decision, that summaries of such witnesses are not appropriate to be led in written form as that's a violation of Rule 92 bis. Furthermore, to the extent that he -- his reports, in particular Under Orders tend to try and conclude legal factors, such as widespread and systematic, such as notice, these are all items that we have I think fully briefed, and so Your Honours are aware of our position and the citations to authority that we rely upon to cite that this is an inappropriate means of getting material in through documentary evidence, and in fact that whether it's qualified as coming in through 89(F) you still have to apply all the other rules that would apply to the evidence if it were being submitted in the other -- under one of the other rules. So I think basically if we look at the areas that we objected to in As Seen, As Told, particularly in the further submissions that we filed just recently, I think the same arguments can be applied to Under Orders, particularly in light of what has been elicited here today and in the prior days' testimony from this witness. So, to be short, I think we'll just adopt those arguments and leave it for the Trial Chamber to consider what the end result of all that would be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic we have already in writing adopted the submissions filed on behalf of General Ojdanic, the submissions of the 31st of July, in regard -- in relation to As Seen, As Told. We would also like to adopt orally the submission of August 2nd of General Ojdanic in relation to Exhibit P2228, the statement of this witness. We have already made our submissions orally in relation to As Seen, As Told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And we adopt the submissions in relation to Under Orders. I would also add that the Prosecution's written submission of 19 July, which we've had reference to this morning in relation to these two documents, As Seen, As Told and Under Orders, I'm looking at page 4 of that submission where the Prosecution identifies the sections which it moves or seeks admission into evidence goes beyond mere recitation of the witness's understanding of a historical context. It also includes such things as his executive summary and his conclusions on the chain of command. And we say he's not qualified to make those kinds of submissions, given his admission that he's looked at a web site and some police and military magazines and he's not a legal scholar or an expert in these areas. So it's more than just history, we say. It goes also to crime base and all the other areas that are listed in the Prosecution's submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is -- are you now referring to a submission about Under Orders, or are you back to As Seen, As Told?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm -- this comment here is in relation to Under Orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 19th of July submission of the Prosecution, remind me what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's the Prosecution's submission in response to your oral direction of the 13th of July where you asked the Prosecution to make its submissions to expand upon three points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's As Seen, As Told.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, they've also addressed Under Orders in that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's in that context you say that they seek to rely upon an executive summary and other matters to which you take exception. Now, have you responded to that in writing or are you just simply responding to that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This was responded to in writing by the Ojdanic Defence team on the 31st of July, and we joined that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that submission deals with that point, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, am I wrong to assume that each accused takes the three points I suppose that are in issue here, the objection to As Seen, As Told, the similar objection to Under Orders, and the particular objection to part of Exhibit P2228, or does anyone distinguish themselves by not wishing to take any of these points?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Sainovic, on the 31st of July we submitted a submission in writing which is a response to the Prosecution position on As Seen, As Told and also Under Orders in which we oppose the admission of both these documents. If they are used, however, we wish to join with what the Ojdanic Defence has stated about this part of the testimony of Witness Abrahams. As for the first two elements, we have dealt with them in our written submission, and on this occasion we wish to join what has already been said as regards the third point that has been raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is that everyone's position? I don't really need to hear from you unless you want to differ from that position. Mr. Bakrac, you want to take a different position, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Last time I understood that it would be useful for the Chamber if we were to state whenever we had a joint position. I apologise if I misunderstood you. My colleague Mr. Petrovic has already said that Sainovic and Lazarevic have a joint Defence submission challenging everything, and we would like to join what has been said by the Ojdanic Defence as regards P2228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does any Defence counsel feel that there is something else to be said on the matter or do we now rest content that everything that needs to be said has been submitted either in writing or orally? All right. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I thought that Your Honour had finished with the Defence counsel. I was wondering if I may briefly respond to one of the submissions that were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The submission in respect to the Milosevic appeals judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And has that not already been addressed? Is there something else you need to say about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very briefly. I would just invite the Court to consider -- I had it right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The submissions by my learned friend is that the appeals judgement would exclude works of the nature of As Seen, As Told and Under Orders. But I would invite the Court to consider the judgement at paragraphs 22 to 24 in particular where a distinction is made between the purpose of the interviews, and the Court held that wherein that case an OTP investigator had gone into the field to conduct interviews for the purpose of a specific trial that was before the Court, then those statements would have to come in pursuant to the rules of the Tribunal, perhaps Rule 92 bis, but that that was distinguished from the present type of situation where the interviews themselves were not conducted by OTP investigators of prospective witnesses for a specific case. And another distinction was made in paragraph 23. May I just read one sentence from that paragraph. I'm sure the Court will consider the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's one of these rather less-than-helpful statements to say that that's different from the situation where the interviews were not conducted by OTP investigators for a specific case. What if they were conducted by someone else who's not an OTP investigator but for a specific case, what's the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If they were conducted by someone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For a specific case before the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these were the statements of prospective witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, that's arguably the position about As Seen, As Told.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, the witness has indicated the very purposes that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that. But let's assume. I'm posing a hypothetical question, and there is an arguable position that Ms. Mitchell was in fact an arm of the Prosecution, as it were. Maybe there were other purposes, but was an arm of the Prosecution conducting inquiries for a specific case, in other words, a case against the authorities of Serbia. Now, what's the answer from the Milosevic appeals judgement to that question? Does that fall within the excluded categories or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would not fall within the excluded categories. I think the sentence I was about to read from paragraph 23: "The fact that the summary," and this is As Seen, As Told, Under Orders, "the fact that the summary has been prepared for the purpose of the particular litigation may be relevant as to whether it should be admitted but as the Prosecution submits it would be quite wrong to submit that or to suggest that such a summary is ipso facto, unreliable." And the Court there made a clear distinction between the situation where the OTP itself goes out to gather evidence and a situation, as in this case, where parties, for a variety of reasons, including what they say is in the interests of justice generally, gathers this information and shares it with this organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you let me see these paragraphs just now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I refer specifically to paragraphs 22 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- to 24. And I think in the judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me. Can I see your copy just for a moment? Thank you. Thank you. Now, is there anything else you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is in that context that the court of appeal referred with approval to the comment of Judge Kwon in the Trial Chamber itself in speaking about the issue. And I quote -- and this is from page T5932 of the trial record. "So to speak for myself, the Chamber is not against accepting any hearsay or summarising witnesses. Take Fred Abrahams, he is a man from Human Rights Watch who made some intensive interviews with a lot of victims. So what we reject with regard to his evidence is only the redaction of the identities of the source of information. But to speak for myself, we are ready to accept him. But this Mr. Barney Kelly is quite different. He is part of the Prosecution team." That's the only reason we are thinking of. So I think therein lies two distinctions; one the purpose that whole interviews were conducted and whether there is sufficient indicia of reliability. If there is that indicia, then it is my submission that the test of admissibility is passed, and it is my submission that the balance of the submissions from the Defence really refer to what weight it should carry. May it please you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the Trial Chamber will consider the various submissions that have been made, both by writing and by word of mouth, and a decision will be conveyed to you as soon as possible. We will now adjourn and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I take this opportunity to intimate a change to the sitting schedule. It's now possible for us to sit for the full day on Thursday, and I think that we ought to take advantage of that this week. It's not going to be possible to do that on many occasions thereafter, so we'll sit on Thursday on the same basis as we've sat today. Now, Mr. Hannis, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Fuad Haxhibeqiri. But before I begin I wanted to raise to Your Honours' attention there are two brief procedural matters we would like to raise with you before the end of the day. They could be discussed in front of the witness, but I don't know if you want to wait until five or ten minutes before stopping time or do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how long will they take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mine is five minutes, and Mr. Stamp has one that is one minute, he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We will do that just five minutes before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And we'll have the witness sworn then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, would you please stand and would you please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I got no translation of that. Is there a problem with the English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me on this channel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I heard a voice asking if I could hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all I've heard on this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I would like to begin with handing the witness a hard copy of his statement, and on the screen we can put up Exhibit P2235 which is the 92 bis package for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, one of the first things I wanted to do was to ask you if you could state your full name for us and spell it, because I understand we've had some confusion about the spelling of your first name.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: My name is Fuad Haxhibeqiri, and it is spelled F-u-a-d, the name, and the last name H-a-x-h-i-b-e-q-i-r-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were saying, sir -- is that the correct spelling of your first name?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The last letter of the name is T, not D. The first name is F-u-a-t instead of D.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you take a look at the document that's put in front of you, sir. This is a copy of your 92 bis statement to the ICTY. Did you have a chance to review that before today?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And apart from changing the spelling of your first name from Fuad with a D to Fuat with a T, are you satisfied that that statement is accurate and truthful to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you confirm it to the Court at this time as your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yeah, it's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is a 92 bis statement that's been offered before. I would like to tender it at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Is it a document which has a number. At the moment does it have a Prosecution number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, it is Exhibit P2235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been referred to, adopted by the witness so it's part of the process with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I had a question about that because I know in dealing with another case where we're trying to deal with appellate issues it was difficult researching, trying to determine when a particular document had come into evidence. I come from a jurisdiction where the magic word "admitted" is said and it's easy for us to find. I know that hasn't been our practice so far in this court, but I would ask if you would be willing to consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's just carry on the way we have been dealing so far, Mr. Hannis, where unless there's objection taken to a document, then it's part of the process once it's been referred to by a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we object to the admission of this statement. I'm not sure if Your Honours have received a copy of it, of P2235, but in particular -- I don't know if we want to make these submissions in front of the witness or not. But we object to the portions in particular beginning at page 6 through 9 where this witness claims to be the chairman of the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in Djakovica, claims to have interviewed over a thousand people, and summarised the information that they gave him. We say that we're in this same situation that we had with the previous witness and our objections to his statement coming in under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the sensible thing for us to do is to follow the same practice as we followed in relation to the two previous witnesses to whom this objection has been taken, and we'll reserve our decision on the matter until we've heard the evidence. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I want to ask you -- first of all, is it correct that you were born in and have lived your entire life in Gjakove or Djakovica town in Djakovica municipality in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you may have to sit a little closer to the microphones. The interpreters say they can't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the time you made your statement, you indicated that you were chairman of the Council of the Defence of Human Rights and Freedom. Could you tell the Court what that council is, what kind of organisation is that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: It is an NGO which was formed in 1991 in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was its purpose or mission when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The purpose of this organisation was to collect evidence mainly on the violence perpetrated since 1990 and even earlier in Kosova up to the post-war years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And any particular kind of violence?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Violence committed by the regime in power. The Serb regime, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many offices were there in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: We had 30 such centres out of 29 communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you start working for them?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: To be precise, in 1995 in July, July or August -- August, I think, rather than July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you continue to work for them?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: For seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to refer to certain portions of your statement. I have some questions that I would like to ask you to amplify on your statement a bit. First of all, in paragraph 11, which is on page 3 of the English, the second full paragraph up from the bottom, you noted that since 1981 that there had been arrests and beatings of Albanian citizens by the MUP in Gjakove but that it had become worse in 1998. How were you aware of this fact of arrest and beatings and of the fact that the condition had worsened in 1998? What was your source of knowledge or information?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: My source of information were the injured persons who came to our office and reported the injuries. There -- these were frequent cases. They were invited to the secretariat allegedly for informative talks. They were tortured there and some of them were even arrested. It happened that due to tortures some of them died in these centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe you mention a couple of those in the next paragraph in your statement. -. When you say "the secretariat," are you referring to the secretariat of the interior, the local police?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes -- no. The secretariat of the internal affairs. This is what I mean. The local police was part of this organ. It was formed in 1998. When I said "due to tortures," I have reported the case of Halit Izet Alija, 48 years old, who was killed because of tortures made on him in this building of the MUP secretariat in January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you to paragraph 14 of your statement, and I think this is the first time in your statement you mention the term "paramilitary." You mention it in the context of the military, the police, and paramilitaries taking part in joint operations in 1998, in April and May. Could you explain to the Court how you distinguish between those three separate forces, the military, the police, and the paramilitary. How could you tell one from another?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I could tell them one from another because they have different uniforms. I have been a soldier myself. You can tell the police because they wear blue uniforms; whereas the paramilitary, they used to wear another kind of uniform, another colour. It was like camouflage uniform. Part of them were distinguished because they wore bands on their arms, and so it was easy for anyone to distinguish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if you mentioned what kind of uniforms the military or the regular VJ wore.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They wore kind of olive-colour uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraphs 16 to 18 of your statement, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you talk about --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting. I'm sorry for interrupting, but we have a bit of a problem in following this testimony -- or rather, Mr. Hannis keeps referring to certain paragraphs. In actual fact, we haven't got any statements where the paragraphs are marked by numbers. Now, is this some kind of internal marking that he has or do we have the wrong copies? I mean, if it's internal it's all right, but I mean I keep looking for this number and then maybe I just shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I should advise Your Honour that I have hand-numbered my English copy and Mr. Haxhibeqiri's Albanian copy is hand-numbered, but I don't have a hand-numbered copy of the B/C/S. I'll try to refer to the page and give Defence counsel a chance to identify by perhaps reading from the first line from the paragraph to them get there. And I apologise, Mr. Visnjic, I wasn't able to get that on the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On paragraph 16 that I want to start with in my English version begins near the bottom of the fourth page, and the first sentence is: "The largest military barracks was on the outskirts of town."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for a long time now we haven't had any translations into Serbian. And by your leave -- perhaps it would be a good thing if you placed your own copy on this thing, whatever you call it, e-court, so perhaps we can follow it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no -- well, Mr. Fila, it's important you draw to my attention any deficiency in the translation immediately it occurs. It's something that's very difficult to go back over. And are you saying that you're still not receiving any? Well, this problem has to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I hear him now -- I mean, I hear it now -- I mean -- but you were looking the other side, so I didn't dare interrupt you. I mean, I'm sorry. Well ... I don't know how else I can handle this, but that's the way it is. Well, I just wanted to ask to have this in English so then we can follow it easier. I mean, say he says paragraph whatever and then we -- I mean, I don't know Albanian, but we can rely on the English for the numbering, I mean through e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think with my rudimentary B/C/S I'm going to be able to give them a reference in the B/C/S version as to the paragraph and page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S version I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think, though, Mr. Hannis let's just think about the fairness of this. The witness is working from a hard copy, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is there any difficulty about putting the B/C/S version on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can do that on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be what's requested to avoid any further difficult with translation, so I think we should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure. And the paragraph 16, as I've numbered them in my hand-copied version, in the B/C/S begins at the bottom of page 4 of the B/C/S, the very last line on that page. But because I used the Albanian as the master for purposes of identifying paragraphs and the various translations in English and Albanian -- and B/C/S do not always make paragraph breaks in the same place, in some instances I've had to join paragraphs to keep the numbering consistent. But I'll try to explain that to my B/C/S-speaking colleagues as I go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in the B/C/S, at the bottom of page 4 of the B/C/S version, the first line is where I'm beginning and for the next paragraphs until the bottom two-thirds of the page. Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you talk about how from August of 1998 and onwards the VJ would shell villages and then the MUP and the paramilitaries would force the villagers to leave, telling them to go to Albania. You say this continued to and during the NATO bombing. What was the ethnicity of the villagers you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They were all of Albanian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then related to that in paragraph 19, which is the next-to-the-last paragraph on page 5 in the B/C/S you say, I'm quoting from the English, "the worst time for this was during the bombing. It was civilian Albanian property that they deliberately targeted." Who is the "they" that you're referring to when talking about targeting Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The Serbs. The Serbs and the Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was it that the problem got worse during the bombing? What changed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Violence was intensified during bombing in response to the NATO air-strikes. Violence and terror start to be perpetrated in a planned, institutionalised way in order to create an atmosphere of fear and of intimidation that make the Hitchcock movies bear no comparison to that, compared to that atmosphere. It was a Hitchcockian atmosphere, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to next go to paragraph 20, which in the B/C/S is the last two lines of -- on page 5. In the English we're on page 5 and about four paragraphs up from the bottom, beginning from the bottom it says: "On the 23rd of March." You talk about when your office was searched and the staff arrested. Were you present that day when that happened?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No, unfortunately no. I left one or two minutes earlier. I don't remember very well. Maybe I left five minutes earlier and I went home. But there were other members, personal members, who continued to work. There were six persons, and once I left the office these forces entered and drove the staff out, beating them, insulting them, and arresting them. They sent them to the secretariat of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that same paragraph you talk about the fact that you had worked with the radio station Voice of America and the Deutsche Welle. Can you tell us what -- can you tell the Court, please, what kind of work you did with the Voice of America and Deutsche Welle.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: We reported on the violence committed at that time in our municipality, about the daily terror perpetrated there. As an NGO, we had a good reputation. We were respected by the public. We were different from the politically formed organisations. We had an independent opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, 21, you mention that: "No NATO bombs hit civilian targets in Gjakove." Can you tell the Court how you know that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: This is true. The city is proof of that. There is not a single bomb dropped there with the exception of the MUP building which on the 21st of May was bombarded, and as a result of that bombing someone who was at home, he suffer -- he was killed actually in his toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated, too, that there was an incident not in the town itself but in mid-April involving a convoy. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Which paragraph you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not a reference in the paragraph, but it has to do with the issue of civilians being damaged or injured by NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 14th of April. That day these forces, I always mean the police forces, and the military and the paramilitary forces, they drove the citizens out of their homes through use of violence, beating them, insulting them, and setting fire to their homes in order to deport them to Albania. Way -- on the way, part of -- some of them died because of the bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Within the town itself, did you -- did you have occasion or take occasion to go around and personally look at all the damage to come to this conclusion that no civilian targets had been bombed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I did go. It -- you mean during the war? The period during the NATO bombardment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At any time. Over what period of time did you do that to come to that conclusion? Was that based on one day's inspection or over a period of months?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: When do you mean actually? Could you explain that to me. What period exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at paragraph 21, and in the English it says that: "None of these bombs hit any civilian areas in the town itself, of that I am certain." And I am just inquiring how you were able to know that.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the NATO had Serb objectives to bombard. They did not have any civilian objectives that they bombarded. This was very accurate. The bombardment was very accurate because, for example, the big barracks close to the Catholic church, which is next to the Catholic church as a matter of fact, the church was not damaged at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, where is the reference to the convoy --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is not a reference to the convoy in his statement, Your Honour. That was based on just following up on the issue of civilians being injured by NATO bombing, and I believe there's a reference earlier in questioning Mr. Abrahams about civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is -- there is nothing in this statement about civilians being injured by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the witness has just given evidence about civilians being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
