utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 21 says: "None of the bombs hit any civilian areas." Then I was inquiring of whether or not there were any bombs that actually hit civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like to hear a bit more about that because the answer is certainly not very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, do you hear Judge Bonomy's question? He would like to hear some more about the convoy in which civilians were killed by the NATO bombing. Can you tell him anything additional about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: On the 14th of April, 1999, during the time of NATO bombardments, these forces entered the area called Reka e Keqe and Lugu i Carragojes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are those areas of Gjakove town?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, in the south-western part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now it might be helpful if we can put up an exhibit that shows the town. It's Exhibit P10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm curious about the relationship between the statement that no civilian targets were involved and this evidence that shows that civilians were in fact killed. Now, I'm just trying to understand how that happened according to the witness and how that relates to his clear statement that there weren't any civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe he's talking about no civilian targets in the town and perhaps -- we'll let him answer in talking about buildings or property. The convoy I think was outside of town, but he'll tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes. I see. I thought this was leading to a suggestion that these were the locations where the civilians were killed, but that's not the case. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Go ahead, if you could, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. You told us that the forces came into these areas of town that you've just named. Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They went into the villages and threatened with their guns -- threatened the citizens with their guns. They drove them out of their homes, insulting them, brutally beating them, driving them into the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if you have yet a map up on one of your screens showing --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have P10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now you see it. Can you indicate for the Judges the areas that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you able to see them on the map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Could you lower it a little bit more. Yes. [In English] This area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what the best way it is for the witness to --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the direction of the border to Qafa e Morines, Ponoshac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there a particular pen the witness can use to mark on the exhibit for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we need to know what he's marking, first of all. I mean, I'm at an utter loss at the moment to know what this evidence is about. So it really needs to be explored in greater detail so that we can understand what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. We are trying to, first of all, establish where these civilians who were in a convoy came from, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, can you show us what parts of Djakovica town you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I said that that part is called Reka e Keqe, that area is called Reka e Keqe and includes 20 villages, and also Lugu i Carragojes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't see those names on the map. Do they appear on this map, the areas that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: No, they don't appear in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where are they from town if this map has north to the top --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: South-west --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the statement, Mr. Hannis, says that Reka e Keqe is south-west of the town and it's a name for a group of villages, and also Dushkaja, which is to the north-east and is another group of villages. Now it now appears we are talking about something which is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are talking about those villages. I don't know if we're talking about the incident in which civilians were killed by NATO bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You do talk about those villagers being driven out of their homes. Can you tell the Court what happened after that and where it happened and how it happened.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: When the convoy, it was a long convoy with villagers, arrived at the place called Meja, the convoy was bombed and several people died.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But apart from that incident during your time in Djakovica, you indicated that you saw no evidence that NATO bombs had hit civilian targets in Gjakove town. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: There is no such case when civilian objects or buildings were bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Excuse me. It was a factory producing refreshments. Part of that was bombed, and the motivation was -- or better to say not -- it was not the motivation but it was a fact that there were police and army forces stationed there and they had heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the factory you've just described?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, in the yard of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, from the time that the NATO bombing began on the 24th of March, where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: From the 23rd when my colleagues were arrested, I left and I was in hiding in the area called Blloku i Ri.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I stayed there for a week in hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: A week later I came back home, I went back home, in the neighbourhood of -- in the old part of the town, where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a name for that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Blloku i Ri.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's where you were initially, and then you returned to your home?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which is in another part of town. Is there a name for that suburb?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: It's called Carshia e Madhe, the great Carshia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see those two areas on the map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I stayed there all the time, with the exception of ten days when I went to another neighbourhood, which is called neighbourhood Hank [phoen]. I stayed there for ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during this time that you remained there until the end of the fighting, you described, first of all, I think on the 25th of March that you saw -- I'm reading now from paragraph 22 which is the next paragraph, you saw police and paramilitary working together in the Carshia e Madhe neighbourhood. You say actually you couldn't see it but you got this information from neighbours who were living there and communicating with you. How did you know they were working together?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I saw them with my own eyes during the whole time of the 78 days of bombardments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In relation to that, paragraph 31 which is the third paragraph down on page 7 of the English and which is on page 7 of the B/C/S just before the dividing dotted line near the bottom. In paragraph 31 you said that from your house you saw on a daily basis homes burning and you said the paramilitary set the fire. First of all, how were you able to see this? How far away were they?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: The houses were 50 metres away, 50 metres or more, but there were some houses which were 25 metres away from the area where I was staying, wherefrom I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many days did you see that kind of activity going on?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: During the 78 days of NATO bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were you able to say that these were paramilitaries as opposed to police or VJ?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: I could distinguish them. I could tell it was them because they had camouflage uniforms and they had stripes and ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You also indicate in that paragraph that there was regular imprisonment of people. What ethnicity are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: They were all Albanians, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how are you able to know that people were being imprisoned during this time since you were hiding out in your house?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI
utterances.text: It was the 7th of May when the fighting started between the KLA and the Serbian forces in the Kodra e Cabratit which is on the outskirts of town, the south-western part. During these fightings, over a hundred people were killed, or more exactly 106 people were killed. Over a hundred houses were burned and 300 people were arrested. Of these 300 people, 150 were released. And the rest were arrested, were detained in a warehouse, a workshop warehouse, in the outskirts of town. So these 150 people who were released, they were released a week later, or better to say six -- five or six days later while the rest ended up in Peja. They were sent there by lorry and bus to the prison of Peja. And because there was no room for all of them there, they were sent to the warehouse of a company called Banana. From there they were transported and sent -- they were sent to the Dubrava prison. At the Dubrava prison, of these people that I mentioned, the number that I mentioned, many of them were killed either by the NATO bombings or because they were executed by the prison staff. So 26 people from our municipality were killed there among the 180 people who were killed altogether there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, if I can, and ask you a question about Gjakove town -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's Mr. Visnjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. [Interpretation] I would just like to make a brief remark. It consists of two parts first. The witness now has exceeded the framework of his previous statement, especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] On one hand the witness has exceeded the bounds of his previous statement, especially the part that relates to the transport of people to Dubrava and their detention right after the arrest. This was something that was not mentioned in his to-date statement. The whole part that relates to Dubrava has already been excluded from this case by your decision, so that was my objection to his testimony here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's of no significance, Mr. Visnjic, because his evidence has made it clear that -- or has not made it clear how it's suggested these people died. So there's no injustice by that reference. On the first point you make, though, there is no reason why the witness should be confined to his statement. If you have insisted, as you have, on cross-examination and the witness is not being presented simply as a -- or his evidence is not being presented simply in written form, then as the Prosecution invite him to give some oral evidence, it's inevitable that that will be on the statement. And there's no rule that confines the witness in that situation to the statement. So I don't think that objection is valid in this situation. And you can take it we will exclude the reference to Dubrava from our minds in dealing with the matter. So please carry on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It appears that -- that Mr. Hannis is actually leading this witness viva voce through his testimony and not -- and not limiting it to adopting his statement. And I think it's inappropriate - Mr. Hannis is free to do that - but it's inappropriate for the witness to have the statement in front of him and to read -- to refer to it and read from it if he's in fact testifying viva voce and not as a 92 bis witness who adopts his statement and doesn't -- doesn't testify from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you give me a reason why that's inappropriate and indeed why it's inappropriate for him to be led through the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's not inappropriate for him to be led through his -- to be led through his testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's inappropriate in my submission for the witness to have a copy --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was given this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, please be quiet for the moment while we listen to counsel's submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My submission is if the witness is going to be led what amounts to -- as a viva voce witness and no longer a 92 bis witness, the witness should not be provided or be given a copy of his statement while on the stand. He should be testifying as a regular viva voce witness. Because I think we've gone way beyond merely asking the witness whether this is his statement and whether he adopts it and asks a few general questions on it. We've gone almost paragraph by paragraph here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, not quite. I'm actually not finding it terribly helpful to have it led this way, I have to say, and I think that must be clear from the questions I've been asking. So from the point of view of judicial efficiency, this is not really an ideal way to do it. I agree with that entirely. But so far as the question of whether it's permissible or not, that's a separate question. So you're saying that in a case where a 92 bis witness is to be cross-examined, then when he's giving his evidence in chief he shouldn't have the statement in front of him. Now, I have difficulty following that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If a witness is being called and led as a 92 bis witness, there may be some -- there's a preliminary question of whether that statement is in fact his statement and whether he adopts it. That's fine. There may be some general questions or additional questions, and I have no problem with that either. But in this case this witness is testifying in relation to this -- what appears to be the entire statement from beginning to end and is in fact a viva voce witness. If Mr. Hannis wants to question him as a viva voce witness, that's fine. But he cannot have the witness statement in front of him while he testifies as a viva voce witness. That's my point. Calling him as a 92 bis witness is inappropriate here because he's actually testifying as a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to agree with the position of Mr. O'Sullivan. The question is put whether there is a difference between hearing a witness viva voce or 92 bis because Mr. Hannis today has glossed over this difference because now we are having the witness testify viva voce and also according to 92 bis. He is testifying and he has his statement in front of him to consult. You cannot have both things. I'm trying to simplify things. This is what I'm trying to say. This exceeds 92 bis first of all with the transport, then with a map that is not there. Now we have heard what was happening at Dubrava and he wasn't there. The main objection of this Defence, Your Honour, and let me finish, I don't want to keep getting up several times, is that we cannot see on the basis of this statement what the witness personally saw and what was later found through the investigation. If he was sitting in his own house, then it probably wasn't burned down, otherwise he wouldn't be sitting in it. Then I don't understand what he saw personally, what he found out as an activist of that organisation. All of this is getting mixed up and it's going to create problems, and I don't think that it would be a good thing if somebody comes to testify under 92 bis and then continues to testify as a live witness. Perhaps if somebody comes to testify according to 92 bis, then there's no need to hear them viva voce, but this is turning into the testimony of a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was a rather confusing submission, if I may say so, Mr. Fila. It started off on a basis I clearly understand, which is to support the point made by Mr. O'Sullivan, and I note what you say about that. But the second point has really nothing to do with that because it's equally relevant to the statement as it is without any elaboration orally and that point has already been taken by Mr. O'Sullivan when he first made his objection. And we will be dealing with that particular point, as you already know, when we have heard all the evidence. It's an argument which you have supplemented to some extent, but it's separate to the point I think that we're dealing with at the moment. Now, just give me a second to consult on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may respond before or after you consult with your colleagues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, just not at the moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, I want to speak in defence of the witness because as far as I was able to observe, I did not see him reading from his statement to answer my questions. Secondly, his statement was given to him in the beginning because as I found with Mr. Stoparic, our second witness, trying to have the witness verify a statement as his own from the e-court did not work very well because we would have to scroll from top to bottom and turn every page and even then he can't see his signature as he can with a hard copy. So that's why it was put to him. Also, to try to direct him to the topic I want to ask him any questions about, it's there so we can refer to a paragraph and see if I'm referring to paramilitaries, am I talking about paramilitaries in March, April, May, for example. And as I recall, this discussion, starting with Mr. Visnjic's objection, that the witness was talking about things outside the statement, and then Mr. O'Sullivan turned to I'm just leading him through paragraph and paragraph, and he's just repeating live what's in his written statement. So there seems to be a bit of an anomaly there. What I'm trying to do is ask him questions that are not in the statement, but I have to go to the statement to say: When you say paramilitaries in paragraph 14, what are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first question that needs to be answered there is are you applying or asking the Trial Chamber to apply Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're asking you to accept his written statement as part of his evidence in addition to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But listen to my question then: Are you asking the Court to apply Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would have thought the answer to that was no. I'm surprised at that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want the best of both worlds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. But what I understood was happening here and what needs to be clear before we go any further is that in light of the fact that cross-examination had been authorised of every witness for whom you made a 92 bis application you sought to supplement their evidence by leading some oral evidence from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that seems to me to be an application of Rule 89(F). And what you're doing is asking a witness to confirm that something which was originally designed for a different purpose is actually true, and therefore he's presenting it as evidence which falls under 89(F) if we decide to allow that package that was originally designed for 92 bis to be submitted in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, then, that may be my own shortcoming in understanding the difference between 89(F) and 92 bis when a witness is called to give -- when a 92 bis witness is called to give evidence or called to be cross-examined and the Prosecution is allowed to lead some live evidence before that begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also clear in 92 bis that the Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement in lieu of oral testimony. And again, it may be that that is what you're doing. If you tell me that's what you're doing, then we will consider 92 bis. But I have to say I don't at the moment understand the objection that's being made that you're not allowed to go outwith the area of the 92 bis statement. The rule seems quite clear. It may be admitted in whole or in part in the form of a written statement under 92 bis, and 89(F) allows a similar process. I, for one, am not desperately keen to get bogged down in the detail of these technical arguments when it seems clear that the practice of the Tribunal in the past has allowed this to happen. And when you look at these two rules together, you can see clearly why the practice of the Tribunal has allowed this to happen. So we'll get into an objection which I think on that basis has been steering us away from an appropriate course to follow. The second matter, though, that's raised is the extent to which the witness has the statement in front of him and we have to be practical about this and make sure that the interests of justice are served. And we have to ensure that the witness isn't inappropriately guided by the statement. Now, he himself has already offered to throw it at Mr. O'Sullivan so he can use it which seems to suggest that he is quite happy to proceed without the statement. You, on the other hand, wish it to be used as a beacon to direct him carefully through any difficulties that there are in identifying the subject matter that you're discussing. You're using it for that purpose, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Only if he needs to to understand my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Correct, correct. So against that background, I think we will proceed on this basis. The objection to going beyond the strict terms of 92 -- of the 92 bis, as you call it, statement is repelled. It seems to us perfectly appropriate to lead oral evidence of a witness, part of his evidence is coming in under 92 bis. And if there were ever any doubt about that, then 89(F) resolves it as long as the Trial Chamber allows you to present the evidence. And since the -- since there is an objection, then we can't take a positive decision finally on the admission of this statement, as you know. But we will allow you to proceed on that basis. And I address now the witness and say to you that, and I think you're perfectly comfortable with this, that insofar as you're being asked questions you should answer them from your recollection and you should use the statement only to make sure that you're understanding the question properly in the way that Mr. Hannis has suggested. So please, ignore it except to the extent that you require to refer to it for clarification of the question, and we'll proceed on that basis. Carry on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and -- thank you, Your Honour. In connection with that, I would just indicate it's my general practice and it was my specific practice with this witness to indicate to him that although he would have the statement on the table with him he should not refer to it, or, if he was, he should advise me and the Court that he was looking at his statement to make any answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps just one final point, Mr. Hannis. It is disappointing that the statement is incomplete in respect of a number of perhaps quite important matters because what happens is you end up with the witness giving answers which really ought not to have been given in light of earlier decisions made -- an earlier decision made by the Trial Chamber. And it's also a bit disappointing that when so much has been committed to writing that we have to have so much oral evidence at this stage. However, we simply ask you to bear that in mind when you come along with the next Rule 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will bear that in mind, Your Honour. I'm sorry to disappoint the Court. I'm looking at the clock, Your Honour, and based on the fact that lawyers' estimates of time are notoriously bad, and we suggested that between Mr. Stamp and I we might need six minutes. I would like to ask if we could stop with this witness for now and deal with the procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not think you will complete your evidence in-chief with him tonight?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not in ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. It would be close, but then I don't think we'll have time for the matters I need to address and one of them has a time-limit that expires at the end of the day that I -- so I need to raise it with you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, just -- there is one thing, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, that I would like to clarify before we adjourn the evidence for the evening. You said that you became the chairman of the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretations] No, I was a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A member from then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war. Immediately after the war I became chairman. At the time I gave the statement I was chairman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are you still the chairman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when -- when did you cease to be chairman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly approach the microphones because the interpreters cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was 2002 more exactly, by the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking you to come a little closer to the microphones. Thank you. So you were chairman from -- from about June 1999 until 2002?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're being asked now to interrupt your evidence until tomorrow. So the evidence will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning. You need to be here ready to continue your evidence at that time. Meanwhile, it is very important that you have no discussion about your evidence with anyone. Now, that is either about the evidence that you have already given or about the evidence you may yet give in the course of the case. Now, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you're now free to leave the court, and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My request relates to the Prosecution's motion for admission of documentary evidence sometimes referred to as the stand-alone documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As you will recall, we filed our original motion on the 25th of May. On the 6th of June there was an order from I think the Pre-Trial Judge to submit some further information, which we did on the 12th of June with a second submission to detail some of those matters on the 5th of July. The Defence then had until the 4th of June to file the response. We did have a number of responses from the accused. Mr. Sainovic and General Lazarevic filed a joint Defence response. General Lukic filed a response. General Ojdanic filed a response. Those were all fairly detailed responses, and Pavkovic joined in Ojdanic's and Milutinovic also joined in Ojdanic's response. Your Honour, we, based on our preliminary view of those responses filed on Friday, it appears there are some legal and factual issues we need to address. We -- our time-limit is running, and we need to seek leave from the Court to file a reply. This is my oral motion to make that request. In support of that I just want to point out to Your Honour one of the things that -- it comes up in General Ojdanic's response. It relies rather heavily on a recent decision I think from the 13th of July in the Prlic case, which we were not aware of at the time we filed our initial motion and supplemental pleadings. So it's some new jurisprudence that we think we need to respond to. We also -- there are some issues raised by Mr. Sainovic and General Lazarevic regarding the fact that documents admitted in the Milosevic trial should not be admitted here because Mr. Milosevic was not represented by counsel. That was not an issue that was addressed before. In that regard, Your Honour, we're simply making our oral motion at this time for leave to file a reply. And given that the Defence had four weeks to file the response, which is longer than the normal time, and given the length and scope of the responses, we would ask to have until the 18th of August to file a reply. However, I would indicate to the Court, in an ever-optimistic point of view, that upon a more detailed review we might decide we don't need to file one. But since today is my last day to file leave, that's what I'm doing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, do you have any objection to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour, from General Ojdanic's Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Fila, I think this concerns you also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no objection. We have no problems with the suggestion put forward by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of General Lazarevic has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, these are the ones referred to. Any other counsel have any comment to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lukic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lukic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we will allow you until the 18th of August to submit a reply if you are so advised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. And that went surprisingly well and quickly, and for once my time estimate was over the actual time. Mr. Stamp has a one-minute matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is something which normally we should be -- counsel I think should be dealing with without burdening the Court with it, but it was raised in court today. And at a previous hearing counsel had asked in court that we provide them copies of the underlying material, the two reports that have been the subject of debates here, and I did indicate that we would try to get them in one case from the organisation that had them and we would disclose what we had as soon as we had permission to do so. So I -- to announce to the Defence what the situation is now in respect to the underlying material for the report Under Orders. The Human Rights Watch legal counsel has indicated that they would make an exception in this case and disclose them after reviewing them to see if there are any extra-sensitive informant, having regard to their paramount responsibility to protect the identities of persons who might be in danger. And so they would be doing that and would be giving us access to the material, so then we could disclose it to the Defence as soon as possible. The Secretary-General of the OSCE has indicated that there are very stringent confidentiality requirements in respect of the identities -- in respect to the documents, the underlying material that was used for the report As Seen, As Told, and we are still in discussion with them for permission to disclose the material. I thought I would just put this on the record since the matter has been put on the record by the Defence, although the Prosecution maintains that this is a matter of material which is relevant but not under Rule 68 or not under Rule 66(A). And if the Defence had sought to use the material in court, they should have requested it long before the witnesses attended so that we could make the necessary requirements. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Well, there's always a sting in the tail of the good news, if that's what you're going to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one other thing. I think under the Rules we are entitled to have those statements for cross-examination of any witness who testifies, whether it's an OSCE statement or a Human Rights Watch statement or a the International Crisis Group that we've also heard about or any other non-governmental organisation that has solicited and elicited statements. Now, we have no such statement for this first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which rule are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I believe -- well, we are supposed to get -- as I understand the Rules, we are supposed to get all statements of any Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but these people aren't -- that's -- I think the point that will be made immediately is that they are not witnesses. You've got the statement of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But also, Your Honour, another point is that some of these statements we don't have in our possession --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that's a separate question. But the persons referred to are persons interviewed, as you know, and on the basis of these interviews a witness has come here to tell the Court what they amounted to. Now, that's different from these people themselves being witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, my -- maybe -- but maybe I have a wrong understanding of this, Your Honour. I had thought that any statement made by a witness, whether it's to the Prosecution or to an OSCE or to a Human Rights Watch representative, those particular statements should also be produced before the witness testifies. Now, if I'm wrong in that, I apologise to the Court, but that's my understanding of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you would have to direct me to the rule that you claim says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. O'Sullivan and I have discussed this, and I believe it was Rule 66, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Rule 66 relates to the statements of all witnesses whom the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial and copies of Rule 92 bis statements. Now, the documents we're discussing at the moment don't fall into these categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Rule 66(A)(ii) -- again it talks about the copies of the statements of all witnesses whom the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but these are not witnesses he intends to call to testify at trial. It's difficult sometimes, Mr. Sepenuk, to get to grips with the system that admits hearsay in principle and then allows abrogations from that in the interests of justice when you're used to working with a system which excludes hearsay in principle and allows abrogations from that in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: These are not statements, though. You mean an OSCE interview which results in a statement, or Human Rights Watch interview which results in a statement, or International Crisis Group interview which results in a statement are not statements, Your Honours, within the meaning of this rule?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, they're certainly not statements within the meaning of Rule 66(A)(ii). They might fall within 66(B), but there the requirement is that they be in the custody of the Prosecution, which they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in some instance witnesses that we are calling in this case actually did make -- did have interviews with Human Rights Watch or ICG and there may have been a report taken from them, but I don't know how these forms are. I don't think they are -- I don't know if they're signed or sworn to or any indication they have been adopted by the witness, and also we don't have them in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, but, Your Honour, we have already received several statements from the Prosecution relating to witnesses who are going to be testifying in this case. And we asked the Prosecution some time ago -- actually not -- within the last several weeks to produce any other statements that they had. So they've already produced a handful of statements. But I would think it's fundamental justice that any witness who's testified and who has given a prior statement, we should -- we're entitled to have that statement. And so far we've only gotten a handful. As to this first witness, we don't know if this witness was interviewed by OSCE, International Crisis Group, Human Rights Watch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This person. The witness right here, the witness who was just excused, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is it you're saying you should have?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If he has made a statement to Human Rights Watch or to OSCE or to the International Crisis Group or any other non-governmental organisation that the government knows about and has a copy of or could reasonably get a copy of I think in all fairness we should have a copy of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would be very surprised if the Prosecution didn't make available to you any copy of such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an e-mail from one of my colleagues that indicates we have 12 witnesses in that position, witnesses that we're calling in this case, who have given a statement to Human Rights Watch or ICG that we have possession of and we have disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I agree, we will and we do, when we have them, for witnesses we're going to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is not a matter that can be resolved here when it doesn't depend on the application of any clearly identified rule. As Mr. Stamp has indicated, the Prosecution are happy to discuss the matter further with counsel and if any further clarification is required, then counsel should direct their inquiries to Mr. Stamp. And if these turn out to be unsatisfactorily dealt with in your view, then you can raise the matter again with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And really the main reason I raise it now is that I understand it that we may get copies of these Human Rights Watch interviews. Now, I don't know if this gentleman is included in that group. But if he is included in that group, then he might have to return for cross-examination, a prospect that no one would like to have happen. That's the main reason I raise it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm in a quandary to understand all this. The point is that a person chooses to make a thousand and one statements here and there. What would be relevant here would be relevant and would even have to produce that statement, statements which have been recorded elsewhere and are not to be used in this court and are considered as classified or confidential statements, of what use are they here and why would they be quoted here, and why should they be produced here? This I couldn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I say with respect, Your Honour, perhaps to end this, with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Unless of course they are used here, then the question of their production and making these available to the Defence will arise, but why would they arise otherwise? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, with respect, because of the rule. The rule provides, 66(A)(ii) that we should give them the statements of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Of all persons who are going to testify. We have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, and maybe I'm missing something, there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, look, this cannot continue as an argument across the floor of the court. Raise the matter, Mr. Ivetic, with Mr. Stamp. If there's another issue to be made because you're not receiving satisfactory information, then you can raise it at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I was just going to state that it's my understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just deal with it the way I've said, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right? The court will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
